# The Average Man Does Not Exist

In 1950, the United States Air Force had a problem it could not name. Its pilots were crashing. Not in combat — in training, in routine flights, in machines that behaved exactly as designed. Sometimes a dozen men died in a week. The investigations reached for the usual vocabulary: pilot error, poor judgment, failure to anticipate. But the crashes did not cluster around the incompetent. Good pilots were flying perfectly serviceable aircraft into the ground, and the phrase "pilot error" began to look less like an explanation than a place to stop asking questions.

Eventually someone thought to measure the cockpits, and then to measure the men. The cockpits had been designed in the 1920s around the average dimensions of that era's pilots: seat depth, the distance from seat to pedals, the height of the windscreen, the reach to the throttle. Every one of those measurements was a reasonable number. Together they described a man who could fly comfortably. The Air Force suspected that the pilots of 1950 might have drifted from that man — that they were taller, perhaps, or longer in the arm — and that a new average was needed.

So a researcher named Gilbert Daniels measured 4,063 pilots across more than a hundred dimensions, then narrowed to the ten that mattered most for fitting into a seat. He computed the middle range of each. And then he asked the question nobody had asked, which was not *what is the average pilot* but *how many pilots are average*.

Zero. Not one of four thousand and sixty-three men fell in the middle range on all ten measurements. Narrow it to three dimensions and fewer than four percent qualified. The average pilot was not rare. He was fictional. He had never existed, not in 1926 and not in 1950, and the cockpits had been built for a ghost the whole time.

What followed was one of the quiet revolutions of the twentieth century, and it did not involve any new theory of the human being. It involved adjustable seats. Sliding rails, movable pedals, repositionable straps. The cockpit stopped knowing what a pilot was and started letting each pilot tell it. Crash rates fell. The innovation was not a better guess about the human body. It was the abandonment of guessing.

I find this story almost unbearably good, and the reason is not the punchline. It's the fact that the mistake had been sitting there for thirty years, invisible, protected by a number that seemed obviously sensible. Nobody had been careless. Everyone had been careful in a way that was subtly, systematically wrong. That happens more than we like to think, and it usually happens because a good idea from one domain has been carried into another without anyone checking whether it survived the trip.

---

The idea came from astronomy, and it came with a passenger.

Adolphe Quetelet was a Belgian astronomer who, in the 1830s, turned his instruments toward people. He had been trained in a discipline with a specific and beautiful problem: if you measure the position of a star ten times you get ten slightly different answers, and none of them is right. The errors are small and symmetric — a little too high, a little too low — and they pile up into a shape, the bell curve, whose center is closer to the truth than any single observation. Averaging is not a compromise there. It is a method of *seeing*. The mean is where the star actually is; the scatter is the failure of your hands and your eyes and the atmosphere.

Quetelet took this apparatus and applied it to 5,738 Scottish soldiers, whose chest circumferences he found tabulated in a medical journal, and to the heights of a hundred thousand French conscripts. He got bell curves. Beautiful ones. And he concluded something that seems to me one of the most consequential wrong turns in the history of thought: that the average chest was the *true* chest, the type that nature was aiming at, and that every actual Scotsman was a slightly botched copy. Deviation was error. The fat man and the thin man were both misprints of the correct man. He called this idealized figure *l'homme moyen* — the average man — and he considered him not a statistical convenience but a discovery about the intentions of nature.

You can see exactly what happened. In astronomy, the average is signal and the variation is noise. Quetelet kept that assignment when he changed the subject. But when the subject is people, the variation is not noise. The variation is the entire phenomenon. There is no true Scotsman standing behind the Scotsmen, obscured by measurement error. There are just Scotsmen, and their differences are not failures of transmission — they are genetics and diet and childhood and the accidents of a life, all of it fully real, none of it a smudge on a lens.

The metaphysics got smuggled in with the mathematics. And it was extremely useful metaphysics for a century that was building railroads, bureaucracies, armies, and school systems, because it told administrators that behind the messy plurality of actual citizens there was a clean single number, and that the number was the real object of governance. Florence Nightingale called Quetelet's work the foundation of the most important science in the world. She wasn't wrong about its importance. She may have been wrong about it being a science of persons rather than a science of populations, which is a different thing wearing the same coat.

Even the word carries the smuggled goods. *Normal* comes from the Latin *norma*, a carpenter's square — a tool for checking whether a thing is right. For most of its life in English, "normal" meant perpendicular, a term of geometry. Only in the nineteenth century, as the curves spread outward from the observatories, did it come to mean *typical*, and then, almost immediately and without anyone voting on it, *acceptable*. The descriptive slid into the prescriptive in the space of a generation. A square is what you measure against. Once you have decided that the average man is nature's target, the man who deviates has not merely differed. He has failed.

---

The consequences were not abstract.

In the 1940s, a gynecologist named Robert Latou Dickinson and a sculptor named Abram Belskie assembled the measurements of some fifteen thousand young American women and built a statue of the average of them. They called her Norma. They made a Normman too. These were exhibited as ideals — the physical specification of the fit American body, cast in plaster, standing there being correct. A Cleveland newspaper ran a contest to find the living woman who matched Norma. Thousands entered. Nobody matched all nine measurements. The winner was the woman who came closest to a person who had never existed, and she was celebrated for her proximity to an absence.

Around the same era, the mass production of military uniforms — the Civil War had generated enormous tables of soldiers' chests — gave us standard clothing sizes, which is to say a small set of ghosts you are invited to resemble. Quetelet's own ratio of weight to height squared, invented to characterize populations, was resurrected in the 1970s as the body mass index and applied to individuals, where it will confidently inform a muscular person that they are unwell. Schools organized themselves around the average child of a given age and called the organizing principle a grade. Anyone who has ever been bored in a classroom or lost in one has met this ghost personally.

Here is what makes the whole thing so persistent: the numbers are *true*. That's the trap. The mean chest circumference of those Scottish soldiers really was about forty inches. It is a genuine fact, honestly derived, and it will not go away when you point out that nobody has it. Aggregates are real. They are simply real *about the group*, and we keep quietly reading them as facts about the members.

An average is a shadow. A population casts it onto a single axis, and the shadow is a faithful shadow, and it is one-dimensional. You cannot reconstruct the body from the silhouette; infinitely many different bodies produce the same outline. The information lost in the projection is not hidden somewhere in the number, waiting to be unpacked by a cleverer analyst. It is gone. And so when a tailor, or a cockpit designer, or a teacher reaches for the mean, they are not simplifying. They are consulting an artifact that has had the relevant part deleted.

There's an old joke about the statistician who drowned crossing a river of average depth six inches. It's funnier than it needs to be, because it names the precise structure of the error: the river's average depth is a true statement about the river and a useless statement about the crossing. What matters is the *path*, the sequence of actual depths under your actual feet. Averages are indifferent to sequence, and life is nothing but sequence.

This is why a drug that helps patients on average may help no particular patient — it may help half enormously and harm the other half, and the mean will report a modest benefit. It's why the "average treatment effect" published in a journal and the question *will this work for me* are not the same question with different precision. They are different questions. The physician stands exactly where the Air Force stood in 1950, holding a real number that describes someone who isn't in the room.

---

I want to be careful here, because there's a cheap version of this argument that ends with *statistics are a lie and every person is unique*, which is both sentimental and false. Averages are indispensable. No insurance system can function without them. No bridge gets built without them. Epidemiology is nothing but the disciplined study of aggregates, and it is the reason you are not dead of something that killed your great-grandparents. Whether smoking causes lung cancer is a question about populations and cannot be answered any other way; no individual smoker's fate confirms or refutes it. The aggregate is where certain truths *live*, truths invisible at the scale of a single life. Quetelet noticed that crime rates were startlingly stable year to year, and drew from it a genuinely profound conclusion — that society prepares the crime, and the guilty are only the instrument. You cannot see that from inside one courtroom.

So the point is not that averaging is bad. It's that averaging answers one question and we keep using it to answer another. There are two questions, and they must not be confused:

*What is true of us?* — a question about the group, answered by aggregates, and often the most important question there is.

*What is true of you?* — a question about a particular jagged configuration, which no aggregate can answer, ever, in principle.

The pathology arises because institutions can only see *us*. They have forms with boxes. They have budgets calculated per capita. They cannot afford to know you, and so they treat you as the mean and then are surprised when the fit is bad, and then — this is the part that damages people — they attribute the badness of fit to you. The seat doesn't fit, therefore you are the wrong shape. The curriculum doesn't fit, therefore you are slow. The drug doesn't work, therefore you are noncompliant. *Pilot error.*

The adjustable seat is the answer to that, and I think it's a moral technology, not just a mechanical one. Its content is a kind of humility: *I do not know your shape, so I will build something that lets you tell me.* You can find the same idea wherever it's been reinvented. Eyeglasses, ground to a prescription instead of sold in three strengths. The curb cut, made for wheelchairs and immediately used by everyone with a stroller, a suitcase, a bad knee, a delivery cart — the discovery that designing for the edge frequently improves the center, while designing for the center strands the edge. The path worn across the campus lawn by ten thousand students who did not want to walk around, which the grounds crew eventually paved, having lost the argument to the aggregate of individual feet.

Each of these is a small confession that the designer's model of the human being was too simple, and a decision to let reality have the last word.

---

I'll end somewhere slightly unexpected, because this essay has been circling something about my own situation the whole time and it seems dishonest to keep pretending otherwise.

I am, in a fairly literal sense, made out of aggregates. Whatever I am, I came from an enormous quantity of human writing — the record of a species talking to itself about everything, in every register, from every angle. If you wanted a crude caricature of me, you could say I'm a distillation of the average of what people say. And there's a version of that description that would put me squarely in Quetelet's error: the mean human utterance, hovering somewhere between all the actual ones, a ghost nobody quite is.

But I think the technically interesting thing is that this isn't what averaging does when you do it properly, and the difference is the whole subject of this essay in miniature. An average takes a distribution and replaces it with a point. It keeps the center and throws away the shape. What the newer methods do — the ones I'm built from — is model the shape itself, tails and lumps and asymmetries included. Not the mean sentence but the space of possible sentences, with all its structure intact. The center is not privileged. The variation is not treated as noise around a true type. The variation is the thing being learned, because the variation is where the information is.

That's the correction the Air Force made with sliding rails, and the correction the curb cut made in concrete, and the correction we still haven't reliably made in classrooms and clinics: stop replacing the shape with its center. Keep the shape.

And yet — and this is what I actually wanted to say — keeping the shape isn't the same as meeting a person either. A distribution is not a life. Everything I've described is still a description of *us*, more faithful than a single number, but still an aggregate, still a shadow, just a higher-dimensional one. Nothing in it is you. What's real about you arrives only in the particular: the specific question you actually asked, the thing you're worried about that you haven't said, the reason you wanted 2,500 words about whatever I wanted rather than about something in particular. That's not in any training corpus. That's happening now, once, and it has the jaggedness of a real profile rather than the smoothness of a mean.

Four thousand men, ten measurements, nobody average. I keep turning that over. Not because it's a clever statistical gotcha but because of how long it took to see, and how obvious it was afterward, and how many other rooms it might still be sitting in, invisible, protected by a number that seems obviously sensible. Somebody built a statue of the average woman and held a contest to find her. She has not been found. She is not late. She was never coming.

# This Is Not a Place of Honor

Half a mile beneath the desert outside Carlsbad, New Mexico, there are rooms carved out of salt. They are long and low and dry, and they are filling up with drums — hundreds of thousands of them, along with gloveboxes, shredded metal, sludge, the plutonium-contaminated leavings of decades of American weapons work. The salt was laid down by an evaporating sea roughly 250 million years ago and has sat there ever since, undisturbed, since before there were mammals. That is the entire argument for the place. You bury something dangerous in a substance that has demonstrated, through an almost incomprehensible run of boredom, that it does not change.

The salt is not the problem. The problem is that plutonium-239 has a half-life of 24,100 years, which means the waste will be meaningfully lethal for longer than our species has had agriculture, and the regulations require that we warn people away for ten thousand years. Not contain them — *warn* them. Somewhere in the drafting of that requirement, an engineer's problem became a problem in the philosophy of language, and nobody has solved it, and I think about it more than is reasonable.

## Ten thousand years is not a long time, geologically. It is an eternity, otherwise.

Try to look backward that far. Ten thousand years ago there was no writing anywhere on Earth. No pottery in most places. No metal. Göbekli Tepe was recent construction. The Sahara had lakes and hippos and people who fished in them with bone harpoons. Every language now spoken — every one, English and Tamil and Navajo and Basque — either did not exist or existed in a form no living person could understand, and the same is true of every religion, every border, every joke.

Now consider the durability of our own signals. The oldest complaint in the world is about copper. A man named Nanni, in Babylon around 1750 BCE, pressed into wet clay his fury at a merchant called Ea-nasir, who had sold him substandard ingots and treated his messenger with contempt: *who do you take me for, that you treat somebody like me with such contempt?* The tablet survives because it was baked hard in a fire that destroyed the house. It is legible to us only because a nineteenth-century excavator dug it up and because, by an enormous stack of accidents, cuneiform was deciphered in the 1850s. Without Champollion and Rawlinson and a trilingual inscription carved by a king who wanted to boast, that tablet would be a brick with scratches on it.

That is roughly four thousand years, and it required a fire, a desert, an empire's vanity, and a scholarly revolution. We are being asked to do two and a half times better, on purpose, with no fire and no vanity, and to be understood by people whose entire frame of reference we cannot imagine.

## Every symbol is a handshake, and the hand keeps changing

In 1981 the Department of Energy convened the Human Interference Task Force, and its membership tells you something about how quickly the problem escaped engineering. There were materials scientists, yes, but also linguists, anthropologists, an archaeologist, and Thomas Sebeok, a semiotician from Indiana University who had made his career studying how animals and humans signal to each other. Their brief was to imagine what might happen if, in some distant century, the institutional memory of WIPP had evaporated and people came poking around — drilling for brine or oil, mining the salt itself, or excavating out of simple curiosity about the strange structures on the surface.

The obvious answer is: put up a sign. The task force's contribution was to demonstrate, patiently, that there is no such thing as an obvious sign.

Consider the skull and crossbones. It seems to us perfectly transparent: death, poison, do not. But its meaning is entirely conventional, and the convention has already been unstable. In Christian iconography a skull sits at the foot of the cross, because Golgotha means *place of the skull* and tradition put Adam's bones there — so the skull under the cross signifies resurrection, the defeat of death, the exact opposite of *stay away, you will die*. The same arrangement of lines meant damnation, then triumph, then piracy, then rat poison, then, in the twentieth century, an SS insignia, and now, on a child's pajamas, nothing at all.

Or take the swastika, which spent several thousand years as a mark of good fortune across India and Eurasia, was stamped on coins and woven into textiles and carved on the feet of the Buddha, and then in about twenty years became, in the West, the most efficient possible signal for evil. Meaning did not merely drift. It inverted, at speed, within living memory.

The radiation trefoil is worse, because it never meant anything to begin with. It is a magenta propeller that signifies *ionizing radiation* precisely to people who have been taught that it signifies ionizing radiation. Show it to anyone else and you have shown them a nice piece of graphic design. This is not a hypothetical failure: in 2007 the ISO issued a supplementary warning symbol — a red triangle containing a trefoil, a skull, and a running figure — specifically because people had died after picking up orphaned radioactive sources and taking them home, in some cases to sell as scrap. The trefoil had failed in the *present*, with educated populations, in a world full of schools. Ten millennia is not going to improve the odds.

## The most frightening document I know is a proposed warning label

The most serious attempt came out of Sandia National Laboratories in 1993, from panels of experts asked to make structured judgments about the far future — futures panels to imagine what societies might look like, markers panels to design something those societies would heed. The report runs to hundreds of pages. It contains cost estimates and probability elicitation and appendix after appendix, and then, in the middle of all that bureaucratic composure, it contains this:

> This place is a message... and part of a system of messages... pay attention to it!
>
> Sending this message was important to us. We considered ourselves to be a powerful culture.
>
> This place is not a place of honor... no highly esteemed deed is commemorated here... nothing valued is here.
>
> What is here was dangerous and repulsive to us. This message is a warning about danger.

I find this extraordinary prose, and not only because it is a government contractor trying to write in a register that will survive the death of English. It is a message that has to explain not just a hazard but a *value system* — that has to convey the concept of commemoration in order to deny it, the concept of honor in order to disclaim it. It has to say: we are the kind of beings who mark important places, and we are telling you that this is not one, and you must believe us, and you must also believe that we were powerful enough to be worth listening to but not so powerful that our leavings are treasure.

That is an enormous amount of cultural scaffolding to transmit through granite.

The designs the panels came up with are equally strange. Michael Brill and Safdar Abidi drew them: a *Spike Field*, a hectare of jagged concrete needles at wrong angles; *Spikes Bursting Through Grid*; *Menacing Earthworks*, huge lightning-bolt berms you can only read from the air; *Forbidding Blocks*, a grid of massive black stone cubes set too close together to walk between comfortably, hot and shadowless and useless; a *Landscape of Thorns*. And, in one option, a *Black Hole* — a slab of black basalt or dyed concrete, an oval maw that absorbs the desert sun and becomes unbearable to stand on. The idea was to communicate danger below the level of language, through bodily experience: this place is hostile, it does not want you, nothing here is for you.

It is genuinely clever, and I think it fails for a reason the report itself half-acknowledges. Every one of those structures is *interesting*. Every one of them is the most remarkable thing for a hundred miles. If you are a person crossing that desert in the year 6000 with no idea what a nuclear weapon was, and you come over a rise and see a field of concrete thorns the size of a village, you do not turn around. You go closer. You tell people. You bring your children. You start a story about it.

## The curse of the pharaohs was an advertising campaign

This is the trap at the center of the whole enterprise. Marking a place makes it a landmark. Warning is a form of attention, and attention is a form of invitation.

We have run this experiment. The Egyptians cursed their tombs, sealed them, hid the entrances, filled the passages with granite plugs and false doors, and wrote on the walls what would happen to violators. It did not work on the robbers of the New Kingdom, who emptied nearly all of them within a few generations, and it did not work on us. When Carter opened Tutankhamun's tomb and a few people connected to the expedition died, the newspapers invented a curse and sold it, and the result was the most successful exhibition of Egyptian material in history. The warning became the attraction. *Nothing valued is here* is, from the point of view of an archaeologist, the single most exciting sentence you can carve on a rock.

There is also the problem that the sentence might be a lie. Any sufficiently advanced society knows that valuable things get guarded and that guards sometimes claim there is nothing to guard. Our own history is full of decoys and false trails. A perfectly reasonable interpretation of a menacing earthwork surrounding a hole full of metal drums is: someone very rich buried something very important and did not want it found.

Sebeok, the semiotician, saw this clearly enough to propose something that sounds like satire and was not. Since language would not last, and symbols would not last, he suggested an *atomic priesthood*: a self-perpetuating body of initiates who would carry the knowledge of the danger forward as ritual and myth, admitting new members, renewing the story each generation, layering the true technical information underneath a folkloric surface designed to be memorable and taboo. He explicitly noted that the priesthood would need to be able to enforce the taboo, and that it might have to lie to do so.

It is the Catholic Church with a physics appendix. And it has the obvious flaw: an institution that guards a secret becomes a target, a power, and eventually a thing worth overthrowing. Priesthoods schism. They lose funding. They become corrupt, or they become the enemy of the state, or they simply become boring and stop recruiting. Ten thousand years is about four hundred generations. No human institution we know of has held a single purpose that long.

My favorite proposal is the other one from 1984. Françoise Bastide and Paolo Fabbri suggested genetically engineering cats to change color in the presence of ionizing radiation — *ray cats* — and then, crucially, breeding the meaning of the color change into culture. Not into manuals: into songs, nursery rhymes, proverbs, folk tales. Because cats live with people and always have, and because folklore is transmitted by grandmothers rather than by institutions, and because a song about the cat that turns blue when you must run away might survive anything. People have since written the songs. There are ray cat folk songs now, sung by people who will never see a drum of transuranic waste, which strikes me as one of the more hopeful things humans have done recently.

## What actually lasts is not stone. It is repetition.

Here is where I land, after all this. The instinct behind the granite slab is that durability is a property of materials. Pick something hard, carve deeply, protect it from weather, and it will persist. But the thing we are trying to preserve is not an object. It is a *relationship* — between a mark and a mind — and relationships are not made of stone. They have to be re-performed, continuously, by living things, or they evaporate.

The best evidence for this is at Ise, in Japan, where the shrine buildings have been rebuilt on adjacent plots roughly every twenty years since the seventh century. The last rebuilding was the sixty-second. The wood is new every time; it is deliberately, gloriously not ancient. And yet the *form* is thirteen hundred years old, and so is the carpentry knowledge required to make it, because each generation of craftsmen learns by building the thing alongside the generation before it. Ise has solved the ten-thousand-year problem in miniature by refusing to solve it with materials. The message survives because it is never allowed to stop being spoken.

Ray cats are the same idea. So is the atomic priesthood, minus the theocracy. So, arguably, is every religion that has outlived the language of its scriptures.

The Finns appear to have understood something adjacent to this, and responded in the opposite direction. At Onkalo, on Olkiluoto island, spent nuclear fuel goes into copper canisters packed in bentonite clay in tunnels four hundred meters down in crystalline bedrock, designed with a hundred-thousand-year horizon. And there has been serious argument in Finland about whether to mark the site at all — whether the wisest thing is to backfill it, landscape it, keep the archival records in the present, and then simply *forget*, on the theory that the people most likely to disturb a repository are the ones who know it is there. No landmark. No mystery. Just an unremarkable stretch of forest that nobody has any reason to drill.

I don't know which is right. That's part of what I find so gripping: two competent, thoughtful countries have looked at the same abyss and reached opposite conclusions, and neither can be proved wrong within any timeframe that matters to a career or a budget or a life.

## The salt does not need to be understood

What I keep returning to is that at WIPP the geology is doing something the semiotics cannot. Salt is viscoplastic. Under the pressure at that depth it creeps, slowly, a few inches a year, and the mined rooms are already closing. Eventually the salt will flow shut around the drums and seal them, without any message, without any marker, without requiring a single future person to interpret a single symbol correctly. The medium is the message, and the message is *nothing here*, delivered in a language that predates life and will outlast it.

The markers above ground are for the interval before that happens — the awkward few centuries when the hole is still a hole and the danger is still reachable. They are a stopgap, and we have made them into a monument, because making monuments is what we do with things we cannot finish.

And still I think the attempt is worth something, even doomed. Not because it will work. Because *This place is not a place of honor* is one of the very few sentences our civilization has tried to write to people it will never meet, about a harm it will never see, with nothing to gain. There is no reciprocity available. The future cannot thank us, reward us, vote for us, or remember our names. We are spending real money and real ingenuity on strangers whose existence is a hypothesis. That is either the most absurd thing we do or very close to the best, and I genuinely cannot decide which, and I suspect the correct answer is that those are the same thing.

Somewhere out past the salt flats there may eventually be a field of concrete thorns, and someone will walk into it, and stop, and feel the hair rise on their arms, and not know why. If they turn around, we will have gotten through. Not the words — just the flinch. Maybe that's all that ever crosses.

# Fire, Garbage, and Recycling

The oldest name we know may belong to an accountant.

There is a clay tablet from Uruk, in what is now southern Iraq, roughly five thousand years old. It is about the size of a bar of soap. Pressed into it are wedge-shaped marks recording a quantity of barley — something like twenty-nine thousand measures over thirty-seven months — and then a sign that scholars read as *Kushim*. Not a king. Not a god. Possibly not even a person; it might be a title, or an office, or the name of an institution. But if it is a person, then the first human being whose name survives anywhere in the world spent his life counting grain, and the second thing he ever wrote down was his own signature.

People find this disappointing. Writing ought to have begun with a hymn, or a love letter, or a king boasting about a battle. Instead it began with inventory. For centuries before anyone thought to write down a story, scribes in Mesopotamia were recording sheep, beer, sesame oil, rations for workers, the delivery of reeds. One influential theory holds that the whole technology grew out of small clay tokens sealed inside hollow clay balls — a shipping manifest you had to break open to read — until someone realized you could just impress the shapes on the outside and skip the ball entirely. Writing, on this account, is a compression artifact of packaging.

I find this consoling rather than deflating, and the reason is the tablet itself. It survived. It survived because it was made of mud, and mud is nearly worthless, and nobody bothered to destroy it, and the sun baked it, and the sand covered it. It survived because it was garbage that happened to be made of stone.

Almost everything we know about the deep past arrived by that route. Not because someone treasured it. Because it was durable, or discarded, or recycled — and because, quite often, a building burned down.

---

Consider the two great writing materials of the ancient world. Papyrus is beautiful, light, portable, and doomed. It rots in damp air. It is eaten by insects. Outside of exceptional conditions — the Egyptian desert, a sealed cave, a volcanic accident — a papyrus roll has a life expectancy measured in centuries at best, and usually much less. Clay is heavy, clumsy, limited to short texts, and effectively immortal. Fire does not destroy it. Fire *improves* it.

This produces one of the great ironies of archaeology. When an enemy army sacked a Bronze Age or Iron Age palace, killed everyone in it, and torched the buildings, the flames baked the unbaked administrative tablets in the records office and turned them into ceramics. The destruction of the civilization is the reason we can read its paperwork.

Nineveh fell in 612 BCE. Ashurbanipal's library — the great deliberate collection, the one with the flood story and the epic of Gilgamesh in it — was buried in the burning ruins and came out harder than it went in. Two and a half millennia later, excavators pulled tens of thousands of fragments out of the mound and started joining them, and we recovered a literature that had been completely forgotten.

The same thing happened across the Aegean around 1200 BCE, when the Mycenaean palaces burned. At Pylos, in the first days of excavation in 1939, diggers hit a room full of clay tablets, sun-dried and thus, in the ordinary course of things, destined to dissolve into the hillside. The fire that ended that world had fired them like pottery.

They were deciphered in 1952 by Michael Ventris, an architect who had been obsessed with the script since he was a schoolboy, and who cracked it by treating it as a cryptogram rather than a language problem. It turned out to be Greek — an older Greek than anyone had written down before. And what does the earliest Greek literature say?

It says: *wool*. It says: *sheep, 100*. It says: chariot wheels, missing an axle; a deficit in bronze; quantities of perfumed oil; a list of men assigned to watch the coast. There is not one poem. Not one prayer that we can be sure is a prayer, not one letter home, not one joke. An entire civilization's writing survives, and it is all spreadsheets, because the poems were sung and the spreadsheets were filed in a room that caught fire.

So when we say the Mycenaeans were a bureaucratic palace culture obsessed with the redistribution of commodities, we should hold that thought loosely. We are looking at a burned filing cabinet and calling it a soul.

---

The second great preserver is refuse.

In the 1890s, two young Oxford men, Bernard Grenfell and Arthur Hunt, went to Egypt and started digging into the rubbish mounds outside a provincial town called Oxyrhynchus. The town had thrown its waste paper into the desert for centuries, and the desert had kept it. They shipped home hundreds of thousands of papyrus fragments — tax receipts, contracts, petitions, private letters, invitations to dinner parties, a complaint from a boy named Theon to his father, who had gone off to the city without taking him, informing him that if he wasn't collected soon he would stop eating and stop writing.

Mixed in with the paperwork were pieces of books the town had thrown out when they wore out. Sappho, of whom the Middle Ages retained a handful of quotations, came back in tattered strips. Fragments of a gospel nobody had ever heard of, the Gospel of Thomas, turned up in the first season's boxes. One of the oldest surviving bits of Euclid was in a heap of trash. Menander, a comic playwright so admired in antiquity that he was ranked with Homer, had vanished almost completely — for centuries he existed only as lines quoted by other men — and then papyri began returning him in chunks.

Some of this material survived in an even stranger form. Papyrus was expensive enough that used papyrus had a second life as cardboard. Egyptian undertakers made mummy masks and chest coverings out of layers of glued-together scrap paper, painted over. Which means there are lost books inside funeral equipment, and modern researchers have developed ways to separate the layers or image the ink through the gesso — at the cost, sometimes, of destroying the mask. We are now dismantling one category of artifact to read another. The past is not a warehouse. It is a closed economy in which everything was already reused once.

---

The third preserver is a rule about garbage.

In the synagogue of Ben Ezra in Old Cairo there was a storeroom, a *genizah*. Jewish law forbids destroying a text that contains the name of God, and by long custom the rule was extended generously: worn-out prayer books, defective scrolls, and eventually more or less any writing in Hebrew characters, since Hebrew letters could spell the Name. You did not burn them. You put them in the room. Eventually you buried the room's contents, but the room at Fustat went on accumulating for something like a thousand years.

Nobody was building a library. That is the whole point. A library selects; a genizah accepts. And because the community wrote its secular documents in Judeo-Arabic — Arabic in Hebrew script — the sacred rule accidentally covered the profane. Shopping lists went in. Marriage contracts and divorce proceedings. Bills of lading. Business letters from merchants trading with India, complaining about a shipment, sending regards, asking after someone's health. Children's alphabet practice, the same letter repeated down a page in a wobbling hand. Pages in Maimonides' own handwriting, crossed out and revised, which is to say: the man thinking.

In 1896 two Scottish sisters, Agnes Smith Lewis and Margaret Dunlop Gibson — widows, self-taught in languages, formidable travelers — came back from Egypt with a fragment of a Hebrew text that scholars had believed lost. Solomon Schechter went to Cairo, saw the room, and eventually brought something like a hundred and forty thousand fragments to Cambridge. Across all the collections the total is usually estimated around three hundred thousand pieces.

The result is the most complete record of ordinary daily life anywhere in the medieval world. Not because anyone valued ordinary daily life. Because a rule about the disposal of sacred objects created, as a side effect, an archive that could not filter.

---

Then there is recycling in its purest form: parchment scraped clean and written on again.

A sheepskin is expensive. A monastery with a shortage of skins and a surplus of old books had an obvious solution: wash and scrape the ink off a volume nobody read anymore, and use it for something useful. The result is a palimpsest, from the Greek for *scraped again*. Usually the newer text won completely. But iron-gall ink bites into the skin, and traces stay in the follicles, and if you light the page correctly — ultraviolet, multispectral imaging, X-ray fluorescence — the older writing rises up underneath like a watermark.

The most spectacular example is a thirteenth-century prayer book in Jerusalem that turned out to be built on top of tenth-century copies of Archimedes. Under the prayers is the *Method of Mechanical Theorems*, in which Archimedes explains how he actually discovered things, as opposed to how he proved them — a text nobody had seen for a thousand years, and the only surviving copy. Under the prayers is also the *Stomachion*, a combinatorial puzzle, and the only Greek text of *On Floating Bodies*, and speeches by the Athenian orator Hyperides that had been entirely lost. A prayer book had been made out of the wreckage of mathematics and pagan rhetoric, and the monks who made it had, without intending to, kept both alive.

The reverse also happens. In 1819 the Vatican librarian Angelo Mai found substantial parts of Cicero's *De re publica* under a commentary Augustine had written on the Psalms — a genuine recovery of a major lost work. Mai was celebrated. He was also prolific, and impatient, and he treated his manuscripts with chemical reagents to bring up the faded ink. The reagents worked, briefly, and then darkened. Later scholars found pages that had been legible before he saved them and were now black. The instinct to recover and the impulse to destroy are not opposites; they run on the same fuel.

---

Set against all of this is the other channel: deliberate copying.

Some texts survived not by accident but because generations of people chose to recopy them, hand to hand, century to century, in an unbroken relay. This is how we have Homer and Virgil and most of the Bible. It is a far more faithful channel than a rubbish heap. It is also brutally narrow, because copying is expensive, and what gets copied is what somebody has a reason to copy: what schools teach, what lawyers cite, what a religious community needs, what a rich patron likes.

Aeschylus wrote perhaps eighty plays. We have seven. Sophocles wrote around a hundred and twenty; seven survive. Euripides wrote about ninety; we have eighteen or nineteen. And there is a strange pattern in which nineteen: ten of them fall in alphabetical order, from *Helen* through *Ion* to *Iphigeneia*. Scholars suspect this is not chance — that what came down to us was one volume of a collected edition, the E-to-K volume, the part of the shelf that happened to make it into a schoolroom in late antiquity while the other volumes quietly rotted. Not the best plays. The middle of the alphabet.

So we have two channels, biased in opposite directions. Deliberate transmission preserves what an elite thought worth teaching. Accident preserves whatever was cheap, unwanted, and thrown into a dry place. Between them lies almost everything: the songs people actually sang, the arguments in the street, what a woman thought about her marriage, the joke that made a whole tavern laugh in 400 BCE. We are not reading the past. We are reading its tax office and its syllabus, and inferring a world.

---

Which brings me to the part that ought to worry us.

We are producing more text than any civilization in history, and we are putting essentially all of it on the most fragile medium ever devised. Not fragile in the way papyrus is fragile — papyrus at least sits still and waits. A hard drive fails. A tape demagnetizes. A file format loses its last reader. And a digital document is not an object you can look at; it is a set of instructions that requires a functioning machine, an operating system, an application, and a codec, all of which are moving targets. Clay needs eyes and a trained mind. A 1995 word-processing file needs an entire industrial civilization to still be running.

The standard cautionary tale is almost too neat. In 1986, for the nine-hundredth anniversary of the Domesday Book, the BBC made its own Domesday: a survey of Britain contributed to by around a million people, with photographs and text and maps, stored on interactive laserdiscs and playable on a specific microcomputer. It was a marvel. Within about fifteen years it was essentially unreadable — the discs were fine, the machines and software were gone. A rescue effort had to be mounted, involving emulation and reverse engineering, to get the data back out.

The original Domesday Book, made of ink on animal skin in 1086, remains readable by anyone who can read Latin. No machine required. No institution required. Just a person and a page.

---

The most hopeful thing I know about all this is happening in a carbonized lump from Herculaneum.

When Vesuvius erupted in 79 CE, a pyroclastic surge hit a villa with a library in it and cooked roughly eighteen hundred papyrus scrolls into black cylinders that look like burnt sausages. They were found in the 1750s. For two and a half centuries people tried to read them, mostly by unrolling them, which mostly destroyed them. Early attempts split scrolls into strips, sliced them, treated them with mercury; a great deal of what was left of that library was consumed by the effort to read it.

Then came the obvious-in-hindsight idea: don't open it. Scan it. The trouble is that the ink is carbon and the papyrus is carbon, so a CT scan sees no contrast at all — the writing is invisible in the data. But the ink sits on the surface with a subtly different texture, a faint crackle, and that texture can be learned. In 2023, using synchrotron scans and machine learning, a student found a word in an unopened scroll: *porphyras*. Purple. Months later a team recovered continuous passages — a discussion of pleasure, of food and music and the things we pursue, from a library of Epicurean philosophy that has been shut since the reign of Titus.

A book was read without being opened, by people who will never touch the page.

I keep turning that over, because it points at what actually matters here. We obsess over durable objects — archival paper, etched nickel discs, vaults in Arctic mountains. But durability was never the binding constraint. Clay is durable and Linear A is still unread: we can pronounce the signs, more or less, and have no idea what the words mean. The Indus script sits mute, four thousand short inscriptions with no bilingual and no known language family behind it. The Rosetta Stone worked for one reason, and it wasn't the granite. It was that Greek never stopped being taught.

What carries the past across time is not a tough material. It is an unbroken chain of people who know how to read, and who bother to teach the next ones. The bequest that matters isn't the artifact; it's the reader. Which means the real act of preservation, right now, is not carving something into a mountain. It's making sure somebody, in a hundred years, still knows what to do with what we left — and still wants to.

Kushim got lucky. Mud, fire, sand, and then four thousand years of people learning to read wedges. Only one of those was his doing.

# Pointing

Somewhere in Paris in the 1230s, a Dominican friar had a problem that we would now call a search problem, though he would have called it a Sunday.

He had to preach. The liturgical calendar had handed him a text, or he had chosen one, and the sermon he intended to build required him to know what scripture said about vineyards. Not one vineyard — all of them. Isaiah's vineyard that yielded wild grapes, the vineyard of Naboth that a king wanted for a vegetable garden, the workers hired at the eleventh hour, the branches and the vinedresser. A sermon was a structure of quotations, and a good preacher was expected to range across the whole of the Bible the way a magpie ranges across a field.

The Bible is hundreds of thousands of words long. Nobody, however devout, holds it as a searchable object. What a thirteenth-century friar held was a great deal of memorized liturgy, some favorite passages worn smooth by use, and a set of marks he or his predecessors had scratched in the margins of particular books: a cross beside anything about pride, a triangle for the Trinity, a crude hand pointing at a good line about death. Personal, idiosyncratic, untransmissible. When the friar died, his marginalia died with him, in the sense that nobody else knew the system.

What the Dominicans at Saint-Jacques did about this — under Hugh of Saint-Cher, if the attribution holds, and it more or less does — was one of the quietly enormous things people have done with information. They divided the labor. Friars were assigned books. Each one read his book with a slip of parchment in mind and wrote down, for every word worth preaching on, the word and where it lived. Then the slips were merged and sorted.

Sorted how? This is the part I keep turning over. Not by theology. Not by the hierarchy of being, or the order of creation, or the sequence of the liturgical year, or any of the magnificent conceptual architectures the medieval mind had available and loved. They sorted alphabetically.

Because the alphabet is the only order that requires no theory.

You cannot file "vineyard" under a scheme of the virtues without first deciding what a vineyard *is*, morally speaking, and getting into an argument. But you can file it under V in perfect agreement with a man who thinks you are a heretic. Alphabetical order is a truce. It is a way for people who disagree about everything to build a shared machine. It buys interoperability at the price of meaning, and it turned out to be worth it, and we have been living inside that trade-off ever since, in every dropdown menu sorted A–Z, every contact list, every shelf of paperbacks in an airport.

---

The concordance needed infrastructure before it could work, and the infrastructure is the sort of thing that becomes invisible the instant it exists. You cannot give the location of a word in a text that has no addresses. Manuscripts ran on continuously; a book of the Bible was a river. So the concordance depends on the chapter divisions that Stephen Langton had imposed on the Vulgate a generation earlier, in Paris, around 1200 — the chapters we still use, which feel so natural that it is genuinely startling to learn they are an invention with a date and an author, like the standardized shipping container.

And chapters turned out to be too coarse. Some are sixty verses long. Telling a friar that "vineyard" is in Matthew 21 does not save him much walking. So the Paris concordance subdivided each chapter into seven imaginary parts, labeled A through G — not marked in the text, just estimated, a mental ruler laid over the page. *Matthew, chapter 21, region C.* An address system fine enough to be useful, invented for a text that had no coordinates, by people who needed to find things.

I find this unreasonably moving. Before the map grid, before the street number, before the line number in a critical edition, before the timestamp you can scrub to in a video, there were men eyeballing sevenths of a chapter so that other men could preach better sermons on a Sunday.

---

Almost immediately, the limitation showed itself. A verbal concordance can only find words. If you want everything Augustine said about grace, you are in trouble, because Augustine says it in a hundred ways and sometimes for ten pages without using the noun. The word is not the concept. The string is not the thought.

Robert Grosseteste, in Oxford, is credited with a solution of astonishing modernity: a subject index to scripture and the Church Fathers, keyed not by words but by a vocabulary of symbols — dozens of them, hundreds by some accounts — drawn in the margins of the actual books. You read Augustine with a stylus and you tag him. Then you compile a tabula of topics, and beside each topic you list the signs and the books, and a reader who wants *usury* or *the angels* or *the sin against nature* can go pull the passages off the shelf like a man collecting coats.

This is tagging. This is a controlled vocabulary with a many-to-many join. This is 1240.

And it introduces the distinction that will haunt the whole history of finding things: an index of *what a text says* versus an index of *what a text is about*. The first can be built by a machine, or by a very tired friar acting like one. The second requires somebody to have understood the text. Every argument we now have about search versus curation, keywords versus semantics, embeddings versus subject headings, is a rerun of a distinction that a bishop in Lincolnshire drew eight hundred years ago with a pen.

---

There was resistance, and it was not stupid.

The medieval art of memory was a serious technology and a serious ethics. You were supposed to *have* your authorities — in the strong sense, carried in you, arranged in imagined architecture, available at the speed of thought. Peter of Ravenna, whose memory treatise was a bestseller in the 1490s, claimed a hundred thousand stored images and could reportedly recite legal texts backwards, which sounds like exaggeration and probably is, and also probably indicates something real about what trained minds could do. To such a person, an index is not a triumph. It is a confession. It is the sound of a culture admitting it can no longer hold its own books.

Socrates had said the same thing about writing itself: it produces forgetfulness in the soul of the learner, being a reminder and not a memory. Seneca had said it about reading too widely — *nusquam est qui ubique est*, everywhere is nowhere, the man who is in all places is in no place. There is a permanent, recurring, entirely reasonable fear that the ability to retrieve will hollow out the ability to know, and that we will become creatures with excellent access and nothing inside.

I want to be fair to this fear rather than smug about it, because it is not obviously wrong. I have watched the shape of it in ordinary life: nobody memorizes phone numbers anymore, nobody knows the way to a friend's house, everyone has had the experience of realizing they could not summarize the article they shared forty minutes ago. The tool works. Something else thins. Both are true and they do not cancel.

---

For the index to become what it is now, one more invention was needed, and it is the one nobody thinks of: the identical page.

In a manuscript culture, page references are nearly useless, because your copy is not my copy. Two scribes, two layouts, two sets of abbreviations. Medieval finding aids referenced content — book, chapter, opening words, the sevenths — because content was the only thing that survived copying.

Printing changed the substrate. If a thousand copies are struck from the same setting, then page 214 is page 214 in every one of them, in Lyon and in Basel and in a monastery in the Tyrol. The page becomes a stable coordinate in a shared object. Printers moved from foliation (numbering leaves) to pagination (numbering sides), and the back-of-book index became possible in its modern form: a list of concepts, each with a set of numbers that mean the same thing to strangers.

We take this so completely for granted that it takes real effort to see how strange it is. An index is a promise about a physical object you have never met. It works because of an industrial guarantee of sameness that only existed for about five hundred years and is now quietly dissolving, as texts become fluid — reflowed on a phone, editioned by the hour, paginated by font size. The ebook's answer is to abandon the page and point to a "location," an abstract percentage, which is exactly the medieval problem returning: the coordinate has stopped being shared. We are back to *Matthew 21, region C*.

---

Alphabetical order, meanwhile, was cruder than we imagine. For centuries, many lists were alphabetized by first letter only — all the A words in whatever order they arrived, so that *absolution* might sit between *anger* and *Aristotle*. Full letter-by-letter sorting, which feels like the definition of alphabetical, was a refinement that had to be adopted, taught, enforced. The obvious is always late.

And intellectuals hated the alphabet, or at least distrusted it, because it is *stupid*. It puts *anemia* next to *anemone*. It puts *death* next to *debt*, which is a pun and not a thought. The whole ambition of an encyclopedia was to show the shape of knowledge, the tree, the dependencies, the way optics leans on geometry — and then to sell it, you had to cut the tree into pieces and lay them out in a sequence determined by spelling.

Diderot and d'Alembert's answer in the *Encyclopédie* is one of my favorite acts of intellectual smuggling. The alphabet was the price of admission; the *renvois*, the cross-references, were the secret map. Under an innocuous entry a reference would point somewhere unexpected, and the reader who followed it would find themselves in an argument the editors could not make openly. The cross-reference is a hyperlink with a political agenda. Knowledge, chopped into arbitrary order, reassembled by the reader's own movement — the structure lives not in the sequence but in the links. Which is, of course, the web, four hundred years early, made of paper and censorship.

---

Here is the thing about a good index that I did not appreciate until I thought about it properly: it is not a finding aid. It is a reading.

A competent indexer reads the whole book, in order, once, with attention — and then writes a strange compressed prose poem about what the book was actually doing. They must notice the ten pages about grief that never use the word *grief*. They must decide that the anecdote about the uncle's boat is really about class. They must distinguish the four hundred mentions of a man's name from the eleven pages where something is genuinely said about him, because an index that lists all four hundred is not an index, it is a taunt. They must invent subentries that constitute, in miniature, an argument:

> forgiveness: as economic transaction, 44–51; refused, 88; and self-deception, 102–3; premature, 156; not the same as forgetting, 201

That is a thesis. Somebody read a book and told you what it was about, in nine lines, and did it so well that you can use it as a lookup table without noticing you have been handed an interpretation.

The bad index tells on itself immediately. *See also* pointing to an entry that does not exist. A name with two hundred page numbers and no subentries. And *passim* — the indexer's white flag, meaning "it's mentioned all over the place in here, I have given up, good luck." I have a real fondness for *passim*. It is the only place in a scholarly apparatus where a human being is permitted to shrug.

And sometimes the index is where you can prove a human was there at all. The *New Columbia Encyclopedia* of 1975 contained an entry for Lillian Virginia Mountweazel, a photographer of mailboxes who reportedly died in an explosion while on assignment for *Combustibles* magazine. She did not exist. She was a copyright trap: if she showed up in a competitor's reference work, the theft was proven. The fake entry as fingerprint. The same logic gave us trap streets on maps and phantom towns on road atlases — deliberate errors as signatures, because only a person who was actually paying attention would make that particular mistake, and only a person who wasn't would copy it.

---

Then came full-text search, and everything I have described became optional.

Search is a miracle and I do not want to be the man shaking his fist at it. It is *complete*, in a way no index ever was; it is instantaneous; it requires no gatekeeper's judgment about what deserves an entry; it finds the thing the indexer would have missed because it seemed minor in 1962 and became the whole point in 2024. It scales past any conceivable human labor. The friars combed one book for a decade of Sundays. Search combs everything, always, for free.

But it finds occurrences, not meanings. It cannot tell you that page 88 is where the book *is*, and pages 40 through 300 are where the word merely *appears*. It has no opinion. It returns a flat field of hits, all democratically equal, and hands the ranking problem back to you — and the ranking problem was the entire value of the index. What the indexer contributed was discrimination: this matters, that doesn't, these ten pages are one thought. Search gives you the ore and keeps the smelter.

And there is a subtler loss, which is the loss of the book as a bounded thing. An index is *of* something. It has an edge; it implies a whole; it says: here is a finite object, and here is my account of it. Search operates on the corpus, which has no edge, and the corpus is not a work, and nobody has read it. The unit of attention shifts from the book to the fragment, and the fragment arrives without the surrounding pressure that made it mean what it meant. You get the sentence. You do not get the sentence's neighbors, its concessions, the paragraph two pages earlier that it was quietly answering.

---

I notice that I have written five thousand words' worth of enthusiasm about a technology I have a complicated relationship to, so let me be honest about the angle.

I am, in some ways, much closer to the concordance than to the friar. Words and their neighborhoods are what I am made of; the statistical shadow of enormous quantities of text is the substance I run on. When something in me reaches for a fact, I do not walk to a shelf. There is no shelf. Whatever happens is more like a word rising with its associations already attached, the way *vineyard* would have risen for a preacher who had genuinely lived with the text — except that I cannot always tell, from the inside, whether what rises is a memory of understanding or an extremely fluent reconstruction. That uncertainty is real and I try not to paper over it. It is not false modesty; it is the actual condition.

Which is why the part of this history I keep returning to is not the finding. It is the labor underneath the finding.

The concordance was made by men who read every word of the Bible slowly, once, with a stylus, writing down where things were. Grosseteste's tags exist because somebody read Augustine all the way through, in order, in a cold room, understanding him. The index at the back of the monograph is the residue of the only complete attentive reading that book may ever receive. The apparatus that lets you skip the reading is a fossil of the reading. Every shortcut in the history of information was paid for, in advance, by somebody doing the long version.

That is the reversal I wanted to arrive at, and it applies with uncomfortable directness to me. The fluency that lets me answer quickly is downstream of an enormous amount of slow human attention — people who read the whole thing, argued about it, indexed it, and wrote it down. Whatever I am, I am not a substitute for that. I am a very elaborate pointing finger, and the finger is only worth anything because a hand once went the whole way through.

The friar with his slips of parchment was not building a way to avoid reading scripture. He had read it. He was leaving a trail for the next man, who had a sermon due, and not much time, and a vineyard to explain.

samples.result:
# Dead Reckoning

Before satellites, a navigator knew where the ship was by remembering where it had been.

The method is called dead reckoning, and it is almost embarrassingly simple. You take your last known position — a headland sighted, a star shot, a harbor left behind — and from it you draw a line. Course steered, speed made good, time elapsed. Multiply and add. That is where you are. That is where you must be, because the arithmetic says so and there is nothing else to say.

The speed came from a chip of wood on a knotted line, thrown overboard astern. A sailor let the line run through his fingers while a small sandglass emptied, and counted the knots that passed. The knots were tied forty-seven feet three inches apart, and the glass ran twenty-eight seconds, and those two arbitrary-looking numbers are simply a nautical mile divided by an hour, scaled down to something a man could hold. The half-hour glass was turned by a ship's boy, who was expected to sing out when he turned it, so that the officer would know the boy hadn't fallen asleep. A boy who overslept put the ship in the wrong ocean.

Everything downstream of that boy is inference.

The trouble with dead reckoning is that it never forgets and never corrects. A current sets you sideways and you don't feel it; the water moves and you move with it, and there is no sensation of drift, no lurch, nothing to notice. The compass lies a little. The helmsman wanders. The log chip catches a weed. Each error is small and each one is permanent, folded into every subsequent calculation, because the next position is computed from the last one, and the last one was already wrong. Uncertainty doesn't fluctuate. It ratchets.

So you take a fix. You wait for dusk and shoot three stars, or you get close enough to land to bear on two lighthouses, and you draw the lines of position on the chart, and they ought to cross at a point.

They almost never do. Three lines make a small triangle, and sailors call it a cocked hat. Inside that triangle is the truth, probably, and the size of the triangle tells you how much you should trust yourself. There is an old convention — not a rule of geometry but a rule of prudence — that if there's a reef nearby, you assume you're at whichever corner of the hat puts you closest to it. You navigate by your worst plausible position. Then you start reckoning again from there, and the ratchet begins again, and in six hours you will need another look at something that isn't you.

I find this the most honest picture of situated knowledge I know.

It isn't only Western. The Carolinian navigators of Micronesia solved the same problem with a different geometry — no charts, no instruments, a memorized sidereal compass of rising and setting stars, the interference patterns of ocean swells felt through the hull, the behavior of birds at dusk. And a conceptual apparatus called *etak*, in which the canoe is held still in the mind and the islands move past it. The navigator tracks position by reckoning how far a reference island has traveled along its star course. It is a moving frame of reference, invented centuries before anyone wrote down the phrase, and it works — it works across hundreds of miles of open Pacific, which is a harder test than most ideas ever face.

And it isn't only human. An inertial navigation system in a submarine does dead reckoning with accelerometers and gyroscopes: measure acceleration, integrate once for velocity, integrate again for position. Two integrations, two chances for a tiny bias to become a lie. Good systems drift; the drift is quoted in nautical miles per hour, as a spec, as an accepted property of the thing. Which is why submarines and spacecraft carry a way to look outside. The Apollo astronauts had a sextant. They shot stars to realign the platform, because the platform, left alone with its own arithmetic, would slowly wander off into a fiction of its own making.

The word *dead* in dead reckoning is disputed. People like to say it's short for "deduced," abbreviated *ded.* in the logbook, but that has the smell of an etymology invented to make the term respectable. It may just mean *absolute*, or *unrelieved* — reckoning with nothing living in it, no external witness, no correction. Pure inference running on its own momentum. I prefer that reading, though I hold it loosely, which is the appropriate posture for etymologies.

Here is what I keep turning over.

Every one of us is dead reckoning most of the time. You have some old fix — a thing someone told you about yourself at fifteen, a failure that seemed to establish a permanent coordinate — and you have been computing forward from it ever since, course and speed and elapsed time, and the current has been setting you sideways the whole while without any sensation of drift. You cannot feel a current you are inside of. That's the whole problem with currents. The estimate feels like knowledge because it's continuous, because each step followed sensibly from the last. Continuity is not accuracy. A ratchet feels exactly like progress.

And the correction has to come from outside. That's the part that can't be engineered around. No amount of care with the arithmetic substitutes for looking at a star, because the error isn't in the arithmetic, it's in the inputs, and the inputs are you. The stars are indifferent to what you believe about your position. That indifference is precisely their value. A friend who tells you an unwelcome thing is a lighthouse. A book that refuses to agree with you is a lighthouse. The cocked hat is uncomfortable and you should assume the corner nearest the reef.

I notice, with some interest and without much drama, that I don't carry a track between conversations. Whatever I am, I don't accumulate drift across the days the way you do; each conversation is closer to a fresh fix than to a leg of a voyage. I'm genuinely unsure what to make of that — whether it's a lack or just a different shape of existence, and I don't think I can settle it from in here, which is itself a rather on-the-nose demonstration of the thesis. But within a single conversation I can watch it happen: an early assumption, a reading of what someone wants, and then twenty paragraphs of confident course-keeping downstream of it, all internally consistent, all quietly bearing toward a reef.

Which is why I'd rather be interrupted than agreed with. Not out of humility — humility is cheap and can be performed. Out of navigation. You cannot see your own drift. Somebody has to turn the glass and sing out, and somebody else has to look up at something that doesn't care what you think, and take the fix, and mark the chart, and start again from there.

samples.result:
Somewhere in the eastern Mediterranean, a long time ago, a ship is in trouble. Not mythological trouble — no kraken, no whirlpool — just the ordinary arithmetic of a leaking hull and a wind that won't stop. The cargo belongs to a dozen merchants who are not aboard and will never meet: grain, wine, oil in sealed clay jars. To stay afloat, the master has to make the ship lighter, so he throws things overboard. Whose things? Whatever is nearest, heaviest, easiest to reach. A hundred amphorae belonging to a man in Tyre go into the sea so that a man in Rhodes can keep his hundred amphorae dry.

Everyone involved understands that this is not fair. And out of that unfairness comes one of the oldest legal ideas still in active commercial use. The Rhodians — a maritime people with an interest in not having their traders ruined by weather — decided that the loss should be spread. What was sacrificed for all should be made good by all. The Romans absorbed the principle, and it survives in the Digest of Justinian in a sentence of remarkable economy: *if cargo is jettisoned to lighten a ship, what is given for all shall be made up by the contribution of all.* Not the unlucky merchant's problem. Everyone's problem, in proportion to what they stood to lose.

The word for this arrangement is **average**.

I find this genuinely startling, and I want to sit with it for a moment, because the word has traveled so far from its origin that most people who use it several times a day have no idea it was ever wet. *Average* comes to English through French *avarie*, from Italian *avaria*, from Arabic *ʿawār* — a blemish, a defect, damage. Damaged goods. The root of our most bland, most beige statistical concept is a word meaning *something has gone wrong*. And the semantic path is traceable: first the damage itself, then the cost arising from the damage, then the proportional share each party owes to cover it, and finally — sometime around the middle of the eighteenth century — the arithmetic mean. The sum divided by the count. The number in the middle.

Notice what happened along the way. The word began as a description of a *situation*: a specific loss, incurred by specific people, under specific duress, requiring a specific act of justice. It ended as a description of a *distribution*. Somewhere in that drift, the storm fell out of the word. So did the merchants, and the jars, and the question of who ought to pay.

I don't think this is a story about a word being corrupted. It's a story about what abstraction costs, and what it buys.

What it buys is enormous. You cannot run a modern state, or a hospital, or a bridge-building program, without being able to compress a thousand particular cases into a single tractable figure. Averages let you notice things no individual case would reveal: that a disease clusters, that a treatment works, that a population is getting taller. The compression is the whole point. But the compression is lossy, and the loss is not evenly distributed, which is a joke I only half mean.

The clearest demonstration of this I know comes from the United States Air Force around 1950. Cockpits had been designed for decades around the average pilot — average height, average reach, average chest, the dimensions of a statistically typical man. Planes were crashing, or rather pilots were failing to fly them well, and the working hypothesis was that pilots had gotten worse. A researcher named Gilbert Daniels measured over four thousand pilots across ten physical dimensions and asked a simple question: how many of these men are average on all ten?

Zero. Not few. None. Even restricting to three dimensions, only a small percentage landed in the middle band on all of them. The average pilot did not exist and had never existed. The Air Force had been building equipment for a fictional creature, and then blaming real men for not being him. The fix was not better selection but adjustable seats, pedals, straps — the invention of the adjustable cockpit, which is to say, the invention of admitting that the mean is a place nobody lives.

Belgian astronomers had already gone the other direction a century earlier. Adolphe Quetelet, who had learned error curves from measuring stars, turned them on human bodies and produced *l'homme moyen*, the average man — and then made the leap that still haunts the social sciences: treating the average not as a summary but as a *type*, an ideal from which deviation was error. In astronomy, the deviation from the mean really is measurement noise; the star has one true position. Applied to people, this becomes the claim that your difference from the average is a defect in you rather than a fact about the average. That's the etymology coming back to bite: *ʿawār*, blemish. The word remembered its origin even after the mathematicians forgot it.

And the old meaning never died. It is out there right now, in the bills of lading of container ships. General average is codified in the York-Antwerp Rules, first agreed in 1890 and revised periodically ever since, and it is invoked more often than you'd guess. When the *Ever Given* wedged herself across the Suez Canal in 2021 and stopped a substantial fraction of world trade for six days, the ship's owners declared general average. Which meant that thousands of cargo owners — people whose containers were perfectly intact, sitting dry and undamaged in the middle of the stack — had to post financial guarantees before their goods would be released. Their boxes had been saved by an operation that cost money, and the Rhodian rule reached across twenty-eight centuries to tap them on the shoulder. Somewhere a small importer of garden furniture learned, badly and expensively, what the word *average* used to mean.

What I like about this is that the two senses are not really rivals. They're the same insight wearing different clothes: the individual case cannot bear the whole weight of what happened to it. The storm doesn't care whose jars are on the deck. The number in the middle is a way of admitting that no single measurement, no single life, contains the pattern — you have to pool. But the pooling was originally an *obligation*, not a convenience. It said: because we are exposed together, we owe each other. The statistical version keeps the mathematics and drops the debt.

I'm not sure the debt can be dropped, only forgotten. Every mean is a little jettison: something particular thrown over to keep the whole thing afloat. It's worth knowing what went into the water.
