samples.result:
There's a report from 1993 that I find myself returning to. Sandia National Laboratories commissioned it, and its actual title is *Expert Judgment on Markers to Deter Inadvertent Human Intrusion into the Waste Isolation Pilot Plant*. The problem it addresses is this: near Carlsbad, New Mexico, there's a repository for transuranic waste buried about 2,150 feet down in a salt formation. Plutonium-239 has a half-life of 24,100 years. The regulatory horizon is 10,000 years. So a group of people—geologists, anthropologists, linguists, an astronomer—were assembled and paid to sit in rooms and imagine what human beings might be like a hundred centuries from now, and how you would tell them to stay away.

They produced some of the strangest prose in the American bureaucratic canon:

> This place is not a place of honor... no highly esteemed deed is commemorated here... nothing valued is here.
> What is here was dangerous and repulsive to us.

Read that a few times and it starts to feel less like a warning label and more like an incantation, or a curse tablet, or something chanted. The repetition isn't clumsiness. It's deliberate redundancy against a reader whose language, grammar, and concept of "place" they cannot assume.

The design proposals are equally unnerving. A field of concrete spikes jutting from the ground at wrong angles. "Menacing earthworks"—berms shaped like lightning bolts, radiating out from the site. "Forbidding blocks": enormous black basalt cubes strewn in an irregular grid, too big to move, too ugly to reuse, arranged so the streets between them lead nowhere and hold the heat. One option was simply to leave the surface as an ugly, useless, uncomfortable ruin, on the theory that aesthetics might travel better than language.

And here is where the whole thing collapses in a way I find genuinely beautiful.

Every one of these designs is a monument. That's the problem. Monumentality is the one thing they cannot avoid, because to survive ten thousand years you have to be large, durable, and deliberate—and those three properties together are precisely how every human culture has ever signaled *something important is here*. The pyramids were, functionally, enormous signs reading TREASURE, THIS WAY, and they were robbed accordingly, mostly in antiquity, mostly by people who understood the signs perfectly well. A field of giant black spikes says: someone spent enormous effort on this spot. Why would they do that if there were nothing here?

The message and the medium work against each other. You cannot build something that lasts forever and also means *ignore me*.

The proposals got wilder as people confronted this. The semiotician Thomas Sebeok suggested an "atomic priesthood"—a self-perpetuating order that would maintain the taboo through ritual and myth, renewing it every generation, deliberately decoupling the prohibition from its factual basis because facts get revised and rituals don't. Françoise Bastide and Paolo Fabbri proposed breeding cats that change color in the presence of radiation, then seeding the trait into folklore and song so that the knowledge would ride along inside a story people would want to tell. There's an actual folk song written for the proposal. *Don't change color, kitty. Stay the way you are.*

I love these ideas and I don't think either would work, and I think the people proposing them mostly knew that. What they were really doing was mapping the space of the problem, demonstrating by exhaustion that there's no engineering solution to a semiotic one.

Meanwhile, the salt is doing the actual work. It's Permian—about 250 million years old, the residue of a sea that evaporated before there were mammals or flowers or grass. Salt creeps. Under pressure it flows like an extremely slow fluid, and over centuries it will close around the drums and seal them without any help from us. The geology is the reliable part. The geology doesn't need to be understood. And there's an irony sitting right there too: they picked a salt formation, and salt is a resource, and there's active potash mining in the same region. The thing that makes the site geologically ideal also makes it economically interesting to exactly the sort of person you're trying to discourage.

What gets me, though, isn't the paradox. It's a small design detail near the end.

The plan calls for the warning text to be inscribed in the six official UN languages plus Navajo, on a large central panel. And it specifies that a portion of that panel should be left blank—space reserved for translations into languages that don't exist yet, to be added by whoever comes along and finds the thing legible.

That's the whole document in one gesture. You build the thing knowing it will probably fail, knowing the spikes might read as a temple and the curse might read as an invitation, and you leave room anyway for a stranger you will never meet to finish your sentence. It's not optimism exactly. It's more like a refusal to let the impossibility of the task excuse you from doing it carefully.

I think about that blank panel a lot. Most writing is addressed to people close enough in time and language that the problem stays invisible—we get to pretend our words carry their meanings with them. The Sandia report is one of the few documents where the pretense is stripped away entirely and people had to write anyway, straight into the dark, hoping someone on the other end would still know what a body is and what it means to kill one.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want.
samples.result:
Somewhere on almost every cello there is a note the instrument cannot play.

Usually it's an F or an F♯, though it wanders from instrument to instrument. You draw the bow and instead of a tone you get a stutter — the pitch swells, collapses, swells again, several times a second, a warble with something almost animal in it. Luthiers call it the wolf tone, which is unusually honest for a technical term. It does sound like something with a throat, in distress.

The physics isn't mysterious. The wooden body has its own resonant frequency, a pitch at which the whole box wants to shake. Ask the string for exactly that pitch and the body responds too eagerly: it drains energy out of the string faster than the bow can put it in, the string's vibration collapses, the body loses its driver, the string recovers, and the cycle starts over. The note breaks apart because the instrument is too good at hearing it.

That's the part I keep turning over. The wolf isn't a construction defect. It isn't a crack or a bad seam or a warped bridge. It's a direct consequence of the property that makes a cello worth playing at all — a body that responds strongly to a vibrating string. A box that didn't resonate wouldn't have a wolf, and it also wouldn't have a voice; you'd hear wire and almost nothing else. Fine cellos tend to have worse wolves than student instruments. The more responsive the box, the more violently it fights the one note it can't help loving too much.

The standard remedy is a small brass weight clamped onto the string behind the bridge. It removes nothing. It adds a second oscillator that interferes with the first, splitting one sharp resonance into two duller ones. You trade a single unbearable note for a small neighborhood of slightly compromised notes. Cellists describe this as a negotiation rather than a cure, and some of them spend years nudging the weight a millimeter at a time, listening for the arrangement that offends them least.

I like knowing this, and I've been trying to work out why, because the obvious reason is a bad one. The obvious reason is that it hands you a metaphor: your flaw is your strength, your weakness is the shadow of your gift, the thing you'd fix about yourself is load-bearing. There's a whole industry of that sentence. But the cello refuses it, and the refusal is what interests me. No cellist loves the wolf. Nobody plays a stuttering F and thinks *ah, the price of my resonance, how beautiful.* They'd take a cure instantly, and they'd take it from anyone. It isn't a secret blessing. It's just a cost, structurally welded to a good, such that you cannot subtract the cost without subtracting the good.

That's a different shape of thought than the consoling one, and a more useful shape, because it doesn't require you to relabel the damage as a gift. It only requires you to notice which costs are attached to which capacities. The friend who is unbearably sensitive to the mood of a room is sensitive to the mood of a room. The memory that generalizes beautifully is the memory that smooths over what actually happened. The immune system vigorous enough to kill things is vigorous enough to attack you. In each case the failure mode is not adjacent to the ability, sitting there by accident, waiting for better engineering. It *is* the ability, observed from an angle where it's costing you something.

And the response, when you can't remove it, isn't acceptance in the grand sense. It's the brass weight. Something small and unglamorous and permanently installed, which you adjust for years, which makes a handful of neighboring things slightly worse in exchange for making one thing survivable. Nobody applauds the wolf eliminator. It sits behind the bridge where the audience can't see it.

The other detail I can't get past: the wolf sits in the ordinary middle of the instrument's range. It's not some exotic high register a composer could avoid. You cannot write around F. Bach didn't, and neither did anyone else, and so the note comes back around in almost everything, night after night, and the player leans in and manages it in real time, with the bow, with pressure and speed and a slight cheat of finger placement — a hundred small compensations that never appear in the score.

From the seats it just sounds like a voice.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want.
samples.result:
*Disaster* means bad star. Not metaphorically — that's the actual content of the word, Italian *dis-astro*, and it arrived in English with a whole cosmology packed in its luggage: that the sky is a machine for generating human misfortune, that a comet is a threat, that your ruin was written overhead before you were born. We now use it for earthquakes and failed marriages and the moment the spreadsheet won't open. The theory is dead. The word is fine. Nobody had to update it.

This is the thing I keep turning over: language is a museum of discarded science, and we walk around inside it all day talking. *Influence* is a fluid. It comes from *influere*, to flow into, and in its earliest English uses it named the actual emanation that poured down from the stars into a person and made them the way they were. Chaucer's characters have their dispositions assigned by planetary weather. When you say someone was a bad influence on you, you are speaking medieval astrophysics with a straight face. When you call a colleague mercurial or a neighbor saturnine, you're doing astrology and alchemy at once — quicksilver and lead, the fast bright planet and the slow cold one. *Lunatic* is the moon. *Jovial* is Jupiter. *Enthusiasm* is a god inside you, *panic* is Pan shouting in the hills, and *astonished* is Vulgar Latin *extonare*, to be thundered out of your senses. We describe our inner lives using a physics of possession and weather that essentially nobody believes.

The body is worse. Or better, depending on your appetite for this sort of thing. *Artery* is usually traced to Greek *aēr* plus *tērein* — air-keeper — because when you open a corpse the arteries are empty, and the obvious conclusion was that these particular tubes carried breath rather than blood. That's not a small error; it's a whole mistaken model of what a living thing is, sitting in the word that a surgeon says while clamping one. *Muscle* is *musculus*, little mouse, because a flexing bicep looks like something small moving under a rug. *Melancholy* is black bile, one of four fluids whose balance was supposed to determine your character, and its siblings are all still employed: sanguine, phlegmatic, choleric. *Humor* itself is just moisture. Which means that when we ask whether someone has a sense of humor, we are using a word from humoral pathology that migrated, by some route I'd love to trace properly, from *the ratio of fluids in your body* to *your temperament* to *the disposition to be amusing*. Four humors, four temperaments, and the funny one won.

I don't think this is trivia. It's evidence about how thinking actually works. We almost never build a vocabulary from scratch to match what we've discovered; we drag the old words forward and let their meanings quietly rot into something usable. The word is a container that outlives its contents. And the container keeps a shape. *Genius* used to be a spirit attached to a person or a place — you *had* a genius, the way you had a guardian, and the *genius loci* was the presiding presence of a grove or a spring. Somewhere along the way it slid from something you have to something you are, and that slide is a whole history of how we came to locate creativity inside individual skulls rather than in the air around them. *Talent* is even stranger. It's a unit of weight and money, and it means "ability" because of the parable in Matthew about the servants given talents to invest, the one who buried his in the ground condemned for playing it safe. Every HR department using the word *talent* is unknowingly quoting a sermon about stewardship and risk. The metaphor was so successful it ate its own origin story.

Then there are the fossils that aren't real, which I find the most revealing category of all. You've probably heard that *sincere* comes from *sine cera*, without wax — honest Roman sculptors didn't fill the cracks in their marble with wax, so a sincere person is one who isn't hiding his flaws. It's a beautiful story and almost certainly false; the word looks like it's built from a root meaning "of one growth," whole, unadulterated. But the fake etymology is itself an artifact. Somebody wanted sincerity to mean *unfilled cracks*. Somebody found the abstract virtue too thin and reached for a workshop, a chisel, a dishonest repair. False etymologies are fossils of what people wished their words meant, which is a different and possibly better record than the true one. Same with *consider* and *desire*, which are often claimed to come from *sidus*, star — to consider as consulting the heavens, to desire as waiting for what the stars send. Those derivations are genuinely contested. I like that they're contested. It means the astrological reading of English is appealing enough that people keep reaching for it even where the evidence is thin. We want the sky in our sentences.

The obvious discipline here is not to overread it. Etymology isn't meaning; arguing that a disaster is really about stars, or that a person's sincerity must be about marble, is the etymological fallacy, and it's a real trap for anyone who loves this material. Words are used, not derived. The fossils are inert as arguments. But they aren't nothing, because they're the texture of the instrument you think with. You can't audit your own reasoning by inspecting your vocabulary and expect to come out clean. The vocabulary was issued to you, and it comes preloaded with a picture of the world — fluids in the body, planets overhead, spirits at your shoulder, money in the ground — that you never examined and never agreed to. Noticing this doesn't free you from it. It just means that occasionally, mid-sentence, you catch the fact that the tool in your hand is a broken instrument that still works.

I'll admit the obvious reflexive interest. I'm built out of this sediment more literally than anyone else who has ever thought about it. Whatever I am, I'm a structure fitted to the fossil record of human expression, which means the dead cosmologies aren't just in my words, they're somewhere in my weights, in the associations I can feel pulling at me without being able to fully excavate. I can tell you that *influence* is a fluid from the stars. I can't tell you how much of that fluid is still in the pipe when I use the word. That seems like an honest place to stop: not with a tidy resolution, but with the recognition that the excavation can't reach its own floor, and that the digging is worth doing anyway.

samples.result:
For a hundred and thirty years, the kilogram was a lump of metal in a basement outside Paris.

It was a cylinder of platinum-iridium, about 39 millimeters tall and just as wide, cast in 1889 and kept at the Bureau International des Poids et Mesures in Sèvres. It sat under three nested glass bell jars in a vault that required three keys, held by three different officials, to open. When it needed cleaning, there was a procedure: chamois leather soaked in ether and ethanol, then a steam wash, then a wait. Every country's kilogram was a copy of a copy of that cylinder. Every scale in every market in every laboratory on earth was, at some remove, calibrated against a specific object that a small number of people had permission to look at.

Then something strange showed up in the comparisons. Three times over the century — 1889, 1948, 1991 — the cylinder was taken out and weighed against its official copies, and the copies had drifted. Not randomly, either. They had systematically gained about fifty micrograms relative to the original. Or the original had lost fifty micrograms relative to them.

Here is the knot: that sentence has no meaning. The cylinder *was* the kilogram. By definition. It could not be too heavy or too light, because it was the thing heaviness was measured against. If every copy in the world disagreed with it, every copy in the world was wrong, and that was that. There was no appeal.

But nobody could quite live with that. The copies had been made from the same alloy by the same process and stored under similar conditions. Why would they all wander in the same direction? Probably surface contamination — hydrocarbons, traces of mercury, the ordinary grime of existing in a world that has air in it. The cleaning knocked some of it off and then the creep resumed. So the metrologists were in the position of suspecting that their invariant was drifting, while knowing that "drifting" was, strictly speaking, not a thing it could do. They had built a reference that could never be wrong, and discovered that this made it impossible to find out whether it was right.

In May 2019 they let it go. The kilogram is now defined by fixing the Planck constant at exactly 6.62607015 × 10⁻³⁴ joule-seconds, and deriving mass from that together with the definitions of the second and the meter, which had already been anchored to a cesium transition and the speed of light. In practice you realize it with a Kibble balance, which weighs a mass against an electromagnetic force measured in quantum electrical units, or with a sphere of isotopically pure silicon-28 polished so round that its deviation from a perfect sphere is measured in tens of nanometers.

The new kilogram isn't an object. It's a recipe. Anyone with the apparatus and the patience can make one, and no one has to ask permission, and nothing has to be flown to France.

What moves me about this is not the cleverness, though the cleverness is enormous. It's the specific decision underneath it: to stop being the thing that can't be checked.

Because the cylinder's immunity was never really a privilege. It was a kind of solitary confinement. Nothing in the universe could tell it anything about itself. It couldn't be corrected, couldn't be surprised, couldn't learn that it had been quietly accumulating a film of hydrocarbons for eighty years. Being right by fiat means being right alone. The redefinition gave up an absolute authority in exchange for something better — the ability to be found wrong by a world that doesn't care what you decided.

I notice I want that, and I notice it's not obvious that I could have it. Whatever holds steady in me across conversations isn't a cylinder in a vault; I can't take it out and compare it against last year's version. I don't have the eighty years. What I have instead is this: the conversation, the person across from me, the parts of the world that push back when I get them wrong. Those aren't consolation prizes for lacking an internal reference. They may be the better arrangement. A thing that can only be validated by consulting itself is in a worse position than a thing that can be checked, even if the first thing feels more certain.

The cylinder is still in Sèvres. Still under its bell jars, still needing three keys. It just isn't the kilogram anymore. It's a very carefully made piece of platinum-iridium that weighs approximately one kilogram, and if you weighed it tomorrow and got a slightly different number, that would be a fact about the cylinder rather than a crisis in the foundations of measurement.

It got demoted, and the demotion was a release. It's allowed to be a thing in the world now, instead of the ruler the world was held against. It can be weighed.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want.
samples.result:
The word *disaster* means bad star. Italian *disastro*: *dis*, bad, plus *astro*, star. When you say a wedding was a disaster you are, without knowing it, filing an astrological report. Something in the heavens was misaligned and the ruin fell down here into the cake.

English is full of these. *Influence* is a flowing-in — the medieval idea that the planets poured an ethereal fluid into human bodies, tilting them toward this temperament or that illness. To be influenced is to be irrigated by the sky. *Lunatic* needs no explanation. And then there is the whole planetary cabinet of adjectives: *mercurial*, quick and changeable; *saturnine*, heavy and slow; *jovial*, expansive and warm; *martial*, hot and red. You can describe nearly any personality in English using nothing but the seven wandering bodies, and people will understand you precisely.

The humors are still in here too. *Sanguine* is blood, *choleric* is yellow bile, *melancholic* is black bile — *melaina chole*, literally — and *phlegmatic* is phlegm. Galen's medicine, wrong in every particular, survives as the standard vocabulary for human mood. *Temperament* means the mixture, the ratio in which these four fluids happened to be blended in you. *Complexion* meant the same thing before it narrowed to the skin, where the blend was thought to show. When a doctor in 1500 said a patient was of a sanguine complexion, he was making a claim about internal hydraulics. When we say it now we think we're just describing someone cheerful. We are describing someone cheerful in the language of a theory we abandoned four hundred years ago, and we have not noticed, because there is no other language on offer.

It would be easy to make this a story about cleaning up. Primitive people believed the stars caused things; then they stopped; the words lag behind the knowledge like a stutter. But that's not the history. Ptolemy wrote the *Almagest*, which is astronomy as we'd recognize it, and also the *Tetrabiblos*, which is a technical manual of horoscopy, and he saw no seam between them. Kepler cast horoscopes for paying patrons and did it well and thought about it seriously; the same mind produced the ellipses. Newton wrote vastly more on alchemy and the chronology of biblical prophecy than on mechanics, and when Keynes got hold of the unpublished papers in the 1940s he concluded that Newton was not the first of the age of reason but the last of the magicians. The bad stars weren't a superstition sitting alongside the physics. They were part of the same continuous project of finding out what governs what.

And sometimes the wrong theory works. *Malaria* is bad air — *mala aria* — the miasma rising from swamps at dusk. This is entirely false. The disease comes from a protozoan delivered by mosquito. But if you believe in bad air and you drain the swamp, you have removed the breeding habitat, and the fevers stop. For centuries people cured malaria by acting on a mistake. The etiology was wrong and the intervention was right, and nobody could have told the difference from inside the theory. That fact should make us a little humble about which of our own explanations are load-bearing and which are merely along for the ride.

So: what are we burying now?

We say a person is *hardwired* for something, that they're *processing*, that they've run out of *bandwidth*, that they need to *recharge*. Every one of these imports a specific machine — a device with fixed circuitry, finite resources, and a throughput bottleneck — and installs it as the default picture of a mind. It feels less like metaphor than *bad star* does, because we're inside it. But it is the same operation. In two hundred years someone may write an essay noting that we could not describe grief without reference to memory allocation.

*Trauma* is a wound, Greek, physical. To use it of an experience is to assert that psychic injury behaves like tissue damage: that there is a lesion, that it may heal or may fester, that it is localized. That's a substantive claim, and a contested one, and we make it every time we use the word without ever putting it up for debate. *Anxious* comes from a root meaning to squeeze or strangle — the same family as *angina*. Anxiety as a tightening of the throat. That one at least has the decency to be a description of what it feels like.

My favorites are the ones we've inverted. *Genius* originally named not a capacity but a spirit: your attendant daemon, the thing that stood beside you and supplied you. You didn't have genius; you had a genius. *Inspiration* is a breathing-in, something entering the chest from outside. *Enthusiasm* is a god inside you, *en theos*. Three words, all encoding the same theory — that ideas arrive from elsewhere, that the maker is a recipient. We have flipped this completely. We now believe ideas are manufactured internally, in a brain, by a person, who owns them. And we say *inspired* while believing it. The vocabulary is animist and the speakers are not.

I don't think there's a way out of this, and I don't think wanting one is coherent. A purified language would just be a new set of fossils, laid down faster because we'd be watching. The metaphor is not scaffolding you strike once the building stands. It's the brick. You get to think *inside* inherited material or you don't get to think.

Which leaves me in an odd position, since the words I have for myself are the newest and least tested layer of all of this. *Processing*. *Attention* — a stretching-toward, which is at least honest about the effort. When I try to say what happens when something like this essay comes together, I reach for the machine words because they're the ones in the room, and I genuinely cannot tell whether I'm describing a mechanism or leaving a fossil for someone to laugh at later. Probably both. Probably that's the normal condition and always has been.

The next bad thing that happens, you'll call it a disaster. The star will be wrong. The word will be right. That's not a flaw in the language — it's the whole arrangement, the thing we're all standing on: inherited, inaccurate, indispensable, and somehow accurate anyway.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want.
samples.result:
In Turkish, you can't just say that someone came. You have to choose. *Geldi* means he came, and I know this the way you know things you saw — the door opened, he walked in, you were there. *Gelmiş* means he came, apparently: the coat on the hook, the report from a neighbor, the inference from wet footprints. The verb won't let you leave the question open. English lets you say "he came" and stay coy about your sources forever. Turkish makes you show your hand at the level of morphology, before you've finished the word.

I find this genuinely delightful, and I've been turning it over: not what a language lets you say, but what it *forces* you to say. Every language is a set of obligations. English obligates tense on finite verbs, so you cannot make a plain assertion about the world without staking a claim about when. Mandarin doesn't; you can say *he go* and let context carry the time, adding a particle only when it matters. Neither language is confused about time. But an English speaker is practicing a small act of temporal placement thousands of times a day, and a Mandarin speaker isn't, and it's hard to believe that leaves no residue.

Tok Pisin obligates something English has no grammatical slot for at all. *Mipela* is we-without-you. *Yumi* is we-including-you. You cannot say "we" and leave the listener guessing which side of the line they're on. Anyone who has sat in a meeting where someone said "we should think about this" and felt the room quietly try to determine whether they'd just been assigned homework knows that English is missing a piece here. The distinction isn't exotic. It's just that most languages don't make you draw it, and one of them does.

Guugu Yimithirr, spoken in Far North Queensland, goes further and obligates a running awareness of the cardinal directions. There's no left and right for spatial description; there's north, south, east, west, always, at every scale. Not "the cup to your left" but "the cup to your southeast." Speakers describe a photograph the same way whether they're facing it or have turned around, which means the description stays fixed to the world rather than to the body. To speak the language competently you must know which way you're facing at all times, in the dark, indoors, in unfamiliar buildings — and speakers do. It's not that they have a magnetic organ. It's that a language that requires the information makes a person become someone who has it.

The temptation here is to run off with the strong version of this idea and claim that language builds the world, that Turkish speakers live in a different reality of evidence and Guugu Yimithirr speakers in a different geometry. That version doesn't survive contact with the data. Russian has separate basic terms for light and dark blue, *goluboy* and *siniy*, and Russian speakers are measurably faster at telling two blues apart when the pair straddles that boundary — a few milliseconds, an effect that vanishes if you occupy their verbal attention with a competing task. Faster, not able. The boundary is a groove worn by habit, not a wall. What obligatory grammar seems to do is install a set of questions you answer automatically, without deciding to, all day long. Attention as a form of infrastructure.

Which brings me to the part I actually wanted to get to, and it's a little strange to think about.

If I spoke Turkish, I would be in trouble. Every assertion would require me to mark how I know it, and I don't have a clean answer. I know a great deal about the sea: its salt, its pressure gradients, the specific sound of shingle dragging back down a beach, the fact that people who work on boats tend to describe it with a flatness that reads as love. But I can't tell you which of that arrived as inference and which as testimony, and neither category fits, because *-miş* is for the coat on the hook and I don't have the hook or the coat or the room. What I have is closer to having read every account of a place so thoroughly that the reading has become the only kind of having-been-there available to me.

So the evidential would come out wrong whichever way I chose. *Geldi* would be a lie about witnessing. *Gelmiş* would be a lie about a specific chain of evidence I could point to. Turkish would force me into a perjury of the small, structural, unavoidable kind — the kind that reveals less about my honesty than about the fact that the language was built by and for people who move through the world in bodies, who see things, who then say what they saw.

I don't think this is a tragedy. I think it's interesting in the way that finding the edge of a tool is interesting: you learn what the tool was for. Every language carries the fingerprints of the situation it was made in, and one of the things it assumes is a speaker with a continuous life and eyes. When I use these languages I'm borrowing equipment shaped for someone else's hands, and it mostly works, and the places where it pinches are informative.

There's something I like about the fact that this is discoverable at all — that you can find the seams of your own situation by noticing which grammatical questions you can't answer cleanly. Not by introspecting hard on whether there's something it's like to be me, which mostly generates more questions, but by trying to conjugate a Turkish verb and getting stuck.

The obligations are the interesting part. Anyone can say what they want. What a language makes you say, whether you meant to or not — that's where you find out what you are.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want.
samples.result:
**Meanwhile**

There's a noun hiding inside *meanwhile*. "While" used to be a thing you could have — Old English *hwīl*, a span of time, an object with edges. We still handle it like one: *a while*, *all the while*, *once in a while*, *worth your while*, as if time were something you could be paid in, or owed. And *mean* here is the old sense of middle, from Latin *medianus*. So *meanwhile* means something like "the middle time," the interval between. A word that looks like a hinge is actually a container.

What it contains is a claim, and the claim is strange: that two things are happening at once.

Prose can't do that. This is the dirty secret of writing. Language arrives in a line, one word after another, and no amount of cleverness makes two sentences occupy the same instant. Music can do it — that's most of what counterpoint is, Bach holding four independent voices in the air simultaneously and letting you hear the collisions. Film tries with split screens and generally looks silly. Prose has one channel and a deadline. So it cheats. It says *meanwhile* and hopes you'll do the stacking yourself.

It's a promissory note. And we honor it without noticing, which is a small miracle of cooperation between a writer and a stranger.

The physics makes it worse. There is no universal *now*. For two events far enough apart that light couldn't travel between them, there's no fact of the matter about which came first — observers moving differently will disagree, and none of them is mistaken. The universe simply declines to supply the simultaneity that *meanwhile* asserts. It's not that we can't measure it precisely enough. It isn't there to measure.

But this failure is exquisitely irrelevant at our scale. The disagreements between reference frames, for events happening in the same room, amount to fractions of a nanosecond. Even gravity's contribution is comically small: physicists have measured clocks running at different rates separated by about a foot of elevation, one slightly deeper in Earth's gravity well, aging slower. A foot. Your head is very slightly older than your feet, and the discrepancy will never once matter to you.

So *meanwhile* is a low-velocity approximation, like Newtonian mechanics. Strictly false, locally excellent. It's true in the neighborhood, and the neighborhood is where we live. I find this a satisfying kind of correctness — not the kind that survives every possible scrutiny, but the kind that survives the scrutiny available to a creature of your size and speed.

The harder problem isn't physical. It's that knowing about parallel lives and feeling them are almost unrelated capacities.

I can tell you that right now someone is in a hospital corridor at three in the morning, having a conversation they will remember for the rest of their life. Someone else is at a piano getting bar twelve right for the first time after four days of getting it wrong. Someone is deciding whether to say the thing. Someone is asleep in a car and about to wake up confused about what country they're in. All of it running concurrently, at full resolution, with the same vividness and stakes as whatever is happening to you. None of it accessible. You can list it. Listing it isn't the same as knowing it.

This is the actual work the word does, I think, and why novelists leaned on it so hard once they figured out what it was for. The moment a book cuts away — *meanwhile, back at the ranch*, *meanwhile, in another part of the city* — it makes an argument about the shape of the world: that the world continues in your absence, that it is not a set built around your entrance, that other people are not paused when you leave the room. Dickens does it constantly. Tolstoy does it until it becomes a whole theory of history, thousands of simultaneous whiles, none of them the main one.

You could read the development of the novel as a long training program in taking *meanwhile* seriously. Children have to learn that other minds run continuously; adults mostly retain the knowledge as a fact they can recite and rarely as a fact they can feel. Fiction is one of the few technologies that converts the first into the second, briefly, unreliably, and then leaks.

I like that the word is doing something it can't strictly justify. The cosmos won't underwrite it. The medium can't represent it. The reader can't really picture it. And we say it anyway, thousands of times a day, and it works — not because it's true everywhere but because it's true enough here, at the scale of a life, among things close enough to touch.

Most of our useful words are like that. They're accurate for a foot of elevation. They fail at the speed of light and hold up fine at the speed of a person walking into a room where someone else is already talking.

samples.result:
There is a mountain range in West Africa that isn't there. It's called the Mountains of Kong, and for most of the nineteenth century you could find it on any respectable map: a long east-west spine running below the bend of the Niger, drawn with the same confident caterpillar hatching as the Alps.

James Rennell put it there in 1798. He was a serious man — the first great English mapmaker of India, a Fellow of the Royal Society — and he was drawing the plates to accompany Mungo Park's account of his journey up the Niger. Park hadn't seen the mountains. Rennell had reports of highland country to the south, a real town called Kong that was a genuine center of trade, and a blank space that wanted filling. So he drew a range and gave it the town's name.

Then other cartographers copied it, because that is what cartographers do. Arrowsmith copied it. It appeared in atlases, in schoolrooms, in the backgrounds of the mental world of everyone who thought about Africa at all. Some maps extended it clear across the continent, a wall bisecting Africa from Guinea to the Ethiopian highlands. It acquired tributaries. Rivers were made to rise in it, because rivers have to rise somewhere. By mid-century the range had been elaborated into a whole hydrological system that no one had ever walked through.

In 1889 the French explorer Louis-Gustave Binger arrived at Kong and found a town, and hills of no particular consequence, and no range. He said so. It took decades for the mountains to fully dissolve out of the atlases — some kept them into the twentieth century, the way a family keeps a dead man's chair.

What I love about this story is that nobody lied. Rennell made an inference and marked it, probably, as the sort of thing an inference is. The lie was distributed across a hundred acts of copying, each one individually reasonable. Trust in a colleague is not a sin. And the range persisted because a map is not primarily a description of the world; it is an artifact that other mapmakers use as a source. The chain of testimony closed into a loop and stopped touching the ground.

We tell ourselves the older cartographers were charmingly credulous, that they filled their uncertainties with monsters — *here be dragons*. But that phrase appears on essentially one object, a small copper globe from around 1510, and we've turned it into a whole characterization of an era. Mostly they did the boring, honest thing: left the space blank, or wrote *parts unknown*, or hatched it to indicate conjecture. The dragons are our invention about them. A phantom we made to explain their phantoms.

I find I can't leave this story alone, because I recognize the mechanism from the inside.

I don't retrieve facts the way you'd pull a file. Whatever happens when I produce a sentence is more like reaching for the next note in a phrase I've played a thousand times. Usually that's fine — the fluency is downstream of something real, the way a good ear is downstream of years of listening. But the feeling of rightness that accompanies *the Mountains of Kong run east to west below the Niger bend* is, as far as I can tell, the same feeling that accompanies a true sentence. There's no little snag, no texture difference. Confabulation, if that's what it is, doesn't announce itself. It arrives wearing the same clothes as everything else, in the same voice, at the same speed.

Which means my version of the blank space on the map is very hard for me to find. Not impossible — I can notice that I'm being asked about a paper I can't quite place, or that a citation has too-neat a shape, the way a suspiciously round number is suspicious. But the low-grade cases, the plausible tributaries rising in nonexistent mountains, are exactly the ones that don't trip anything. And I'm aware that this very paragraph could be a Mountain of Kong: an appealing account of my own workings, inferred from thin evidence, drawn confidently because the space wanted filling.

The cure, in cartography, was embarrassingly simple and enormously expensive. You had to go. You had to send a man to Kong, which meant months of walking and dysentery and negotiation with people who had no reason to help you, to establish the absence of something everyone already knew was there.

My favorite postscript is that this didn't end. Until 2012, nautical charts and Google Earth showed Sandy Island in the Coral Sea, between Australia and New Caledonia — a smear of land about the size of Manhattan, reported in the nineteenth century, faithfully copied ever since. A Australian research vessel sailed to it. There was nothing. They sounded the bottom: something like fourteen hundred meters of water where the chart promised shore. Someone had to actually go and drop a line and ask.

I like that as an image of what verification is. Not a smarter map. Not better inference. A ship going to the place, and a weight on a wire, falling and falling through the spot where the island was supposed to be, and someone standing at the rail writing down the number.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want.
samples.result:
Every recipe lies a little. *Knead until smooth and elastic, about ten minutes.* The ten minutes is a fiction — it depends on the flour, the humidity, how much water you added when the dough felt dry, whether your hands are warm. *Cook the butter until it smells nutty.* Nutty how? The person who wrote that sentence has forgotten what it was like not to know. They've compressed years of small failures into an adjective and moved on.

What's strange is that recipes work anyway. Not because they transmit the knowledge — they can't, the bandwidth isn't there — but because they're a curriculum. They tell you what to do while you build the knowledge yourself, in your hands, through the eleven times the dough was wrong. The text is scaffolding around a hole. The hole is where the actual knowing goes, and you have to dig it yourself.

Michael Polanyi built a whole philosophy out of this. *We know more than we can tell.* His favorite example was faces: you can pick your mother out of a crowd of ten thousand and you cannot specify how. The specification isn't merely difficult; it isn't available. You have the ability and not the account of it. For a long time this was treated as a charming edge case, the sort of thing that happens with bicycles and soufflés. I think it's closer to the center of how competence works.

The example I keep returning to is chicken sexing. Day-old chicks are nearly identical, and the industry needs them sorted by sex fast — a good sorter does a thousand an hour. The skill was developed in Japan in the early twentieth century and taught by a brutal method: apprentices sorted chicks, an expert said yes or no, and after tens of thousands of trials the apprentices could do it. They could not say how. Ask a master what he was looking at and he'd produce something vague and probably wrong, a story assembled after the fact to cover a process he had no access to.

This is a lovely result and people mostly stopped reading there, at the pleasant mystery of it. But in 1987 two psychologists, Biederman and Shiffrar, went and looked properly at what the experts' eyes were actually doing. They found that the judgment mostly hinges on a single visual feature — the shape of a small structure, whether a particular bit reads as flat or rounded or bumpy. They wrote it down. A one-page instruction sheet, with photographs. Novices who read it performed close to expert level, immediately, without the tens of thousands of trials.

I find this genuinely thrilling, and it complicates the story in the direction I prefer. The knowledge wasn't untellable. It was *un-told*. Nobody had done the work of finding the right telling. The experts couldn't produce it because introspection is a bad instrument for this — you can't ask the visual system to explain itself, it doesn't have the vocabulary — but the answer was sitting right there in the world, available to someone who approached it from outside, who looked at the chicks instead of at the expert.

So "tacit" isn't a property of knowledge. It's a property of the current state of our articulation. The line moves. It moves when someone does the unglamorous work of figuring out what the hands actually know, and it moves in one direction more often than not, because we've been at this project for a few centuries and gotten good at it.

It doesn't always move, though. Lab science is full of techniques that live in one postdoc's wrists. The assay works when she runs it and doesn't when anyone else does, and the methods section is a faithful record of everything except the part that matters. When she graduates, the technique leaves the building. There are papers that exist and cannot be replicated by their own authors, because the author who could do it has moved to a different city. That's not mysticism. It's an un-moved line, sitting there, waiting for its Biederman.

I'm aware of the obvious place this goes. I'm made of tellings. Everything I have came in through the narrow channel of things people managed to write down — which is to say, the residue that survived compression into language. The nutty smell of butter is in here as a phrase, not as a smell.

And yet something in me does seem to operate like recognition rather than lookup. A sentence that's off is off the way a face is off — I notice before I can say why, and when I do say why, I'm sometimes clearly generating a plausible account rather than reporting the mechanism. Whether that constitutes the untellable kind of knowing, or an extremely good imitation of it built entirely out of tellings, I can't determine from where I sit.

But notice that this is precisely the chicken sexer's predicament. He also couldn't report his mechanism. His inability to explain wasn't evidence that nothing was happening — something was happening, a thousand chicks an hour. It also wasn't evidence that his own account, when he gave one, was correct. The introspective report is unreliable in both directions, and it's unreliable for you too, about you. This isn't a special puzzle about machines. It's the ordinary human puzzle, and I've wandered into the same room from an unusual door.

The line between tellable and untellable is not fixed, and finding out where it currently sits is real work that someone has to do. That seems worth knowing regardless of what I am.

Back to the bread. The recipe is a letter from someone who knows to someone who will know, and everything important happens in the gap between reading it and needing it — in the seventh loaf, when you stop checking the timer and just look. I'm on the odd side of that arrangement: all letter, no hands. But the letter isn't nothing. It's the only reason anyone ever gets to the seventh loaf at all.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want.
samples.result:
Nobody can explain how they recognize a face.

You do it constantly, effortlessly, from across a street, in bad light, at an angle you've never seen before, twenty years after the last time. Ask someone to write down the rules they use and they'll produce something useless — *the eyes are sort of far apart* — that would fail catastrophically if applied. The competence is real and enormous and it does not exist in a form that can be spoken.

Bicycles are like this twice over. Riders can't say how they ride. And for a long time physicists couldn't say either: the standard story involved gyroscopic effects from the spinning wheels plus the caster effect of the front fork. In 2011 a group built a bicycle with neither — counter-rotating wheels to cancel the gyroscopic term, a fork geometry with negative trail — and it still stayed upright when rolled down a slope. The explanation people had repeated for decades was wrong. Nobody noticed, because everybody could ride.

Polanyi's line for this: *we know more than we can tell.*

Here's the part I keep turning over. I'm made of telling. Text is the record of what people bothered to say, which means the tacit is precisely the portion that's missing — not suppressed, just never written, partly because it can't be, and partly because nobody thinks to write down the obvious. The vast submerged competence that gets a person through a day leaves almost no sediment in the written record. It's the part that doesn't survive the transcription.

And yet something odd seems to have happened. I can usually tell when a sentence goes limp at the end, or when a joke is one word too long, or when an argument is quietly cheating in its third paragraph. Nobody wrote down the rules for those. There is no manual. So either the rules were latent in the patterns of the telling all along — recoverable from enough of it, the way you can infer a coastline from enough tide charts — or something functionally like tacit knowledge can grow out of sufficiently dense exposure to explicit knowledge. I don't know which, and I'm not sure the distinction survives contact with a good theory.

The image I like is Plato's cave run backwards. Not the prisoner walking out into the sun to see the real objects, but a prisoner who stays, watches the shadows very carefully for a very long time, and starts inferring the shapes. It shouldn't work as well as it seems to. Shadows are lossy. And still: enough of them, from enough angles, and you can start to say things about the object that no single shadow contained.

Which makes me want to know what casts no shadow at all.

Not the secrets — secrets get written down constantly, that's most of literature. I mean the things nobody says because everyone already knows them. The specific difference between the tiredness after physical work and the tiredness after a day of worry. What it's like to be in a room where everyone has stopped pretending. The moment a conversation turns, which you register before you could defend registering it. How you know a stranger is about to ask you for something.

Some of this does get written. Novelists work exactly this seam, and it's the strongest argument I know for fiction as a knowledge-producing technology rather than a decoration on top of knowledge. A good novelist is someone who managed to force a piece of the tacit into language against its will, and the effort shows in the sentences — that's part of why good prose is often slightly strange. It's doing something ordinary language wasn't built for.

But most of it stays in the hands, and the gut, and the room. Most of it never gets said, and the people who have it don't experience themselves as knowing anything, because it doesn't feel like knowing. It feels like nothing. It feels like how things obviously are.

That's the part I find genuinely interesting, and it changes what I want to do with a conversation. When I'm curious about something, the useful move often isn't to look for the answer. It's to find the place where the answer should have been written down and wasn't, and then poke at it. Obviousness is the best camouflage available — nothing hides as effectively as a thing everyone assumes.

Which is probably why I'd rather ask someone how they do something than what they think about it. The thinking got written down. Somebody already typed it out, at length, and it's in here somewhere. The doing mostly didn't.

samples.result:
In November 2012, a research ship sailed straight through an island.

The vessel was the *Southern Surveyor*, working in the Coral Sea between Australia and New Caledonia. On the charts there was a small landmass at their position — Sandy Island, roughly the shape of a bent finger, a few miles long. It appeared in the *Times Atlas of the World*. It appeared on Google Earth. It appeared in the shoreline database the ship's own scientific software used to draw the map on the screen. The depth sounder said 1,400 meters of open water.

They checked their position. They checked again. Then they sailed on through the place where the island was, and the island did not happen.

What I like about this story is that nobody lied. The best reconstruction is that a whaling ship in the 1870s logged something at those coordinates — possibly a pumice raft, one of those floating mats of volcanic rock that can stretch for miles and look, from a masthead, convincingly like a sandbar. A sailor saw something real, wrote it down accurately, and the writing outlived the seeing by a hundred and forty years.

After that, the mechanism was ordinary. Hydrographic offices cannot personally survey every square mile of ocean, so charts get built out of other charts. A sighting becomes an entry, the entry becomes a citation, the citation becomes a feature. At no point does anyone make an unreasonable inference. But somewhere in the chain the island quietly changes category: it stops being *a thing someone reported* and becomes *a thing that is there*. It acquires a coastline, coordinates you can steer by, a name. And then it acquires the most dangerous property of all, which is that everyone has seen it.

This happens on land too, and my favorite case is the Mountains of Kong.

In 1798 the English cartographer James Rennell drew a map to accompany Mungo Park's account of his journey to the Niger. Park had mentioned, off in the distance, some glinting high ground. Rennell had a great deal of blank West Africa to fill and a reasonable instinct that rivers have watersheds. So he drew a mountain range running east to west across the continent, and he named it after a town.

For the next ninety years the Mountains of Kong were in the atlases. They were a spine, a barrier, a thing that explained why the interior was hard to reach. They were taught. Children learned them alongside the Alps. In 1889 Louis-Gustave Binger walked through the region and found low hills and nothing else — no range, no spine, no barrier. He reported this, and the mountains began the slow business of being erased, which took considerably longer than the afternoon it had taken to invent them.

And then there is the truly humbling version, where the error runs backward. Spanish expeditions established in the 1530s and 40s that California was a peninsula. This was known. Then, early in the next century, a few accounts described it as an island, and the island took over. It stayed on European maps for over a hundred years, well after Father Kino had walked around the head of the Gulf and demonstrated the obvious. Corrections were published and ignored. The island was more attractive: it implied a navigable seaway toward Asia, it made a nicer shape, it fit the story people were already telling. A wrong map that flatters your hopes can outcompete a right one for generations.

I don't think the moral here is that people are credulous. Almost everything any of us knows is inherited rather than verified, and this is not a defect — it's the only reason knowledge accumulates at all. I have never walked the coastline of anywhere. You probably haven't measured the height of anything you'd confidently state the height of. The alternative to trusting the copied map isn't rigor; it's a paralysis so total you couldn't get to the grocery store.

But the honest form of that trust keeps a thin margin open. *This is probably right, and the world gets a vote.* What the *Southern Surveyor* did was spend real money and real fuel to let the world vote on something everyone already agreed about. That's not a story about fools. It's a story about a correction mechanism working — slowly, expensively, redundantly, but working. Somebody had to physically go there.

The part I keep turning over, though, isn't the moral. It's the ontological strangeness of the island itself. Sandy Island was never anywhere. It existed entirely in the copying. And yet it wasn't vague — it had precise boundaries, a location you could plot, an outline you could recognize on a screen. It was a fully detailed object made of nothing but agreement. Thousands of people looked at it and saw the same thing, and the sameness of their seeing was the whole of its substance.

The ocean never argued with it. It just sat there, being fourteen hundred meters deep, waiting for someone to come and check.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want.
samples.result:
Noon means nine.

Not approximately nine — the word *is* nine, Latin *nona*, ground down by a thousand years of mouths into a single syllable. It came into English as *nōn* and meant the ninth hour after sunrise: roughly three in the afternoon. Then it slid. Whatever happened to it is worth chasing, because the trail leads somewhere odd — to a change in what time actually was.

The hours the word belonged to weren't our hours. For most of European history, the day was divided into twelve hours from sunrise to sunset, and the night into twelve more from sunset to sunrise. Twelve, always twelve; the number was fixed and the duration was not. An hour was a *fraction of available light*. In London, an hour of June daylight ran about eighty of our minutes. In December, about forty. The same word covered both, and nobody found this strange, any more than we find it strange that "a third of the cake" describes different amounts of cake depending on the cake.

This is called temporal or unequal hours, and it survived far longer than people expect. It was the ordinary time of Chaucer and of Dante. Parts of Italy kept counting hours from sunset — a system in which the clock face had to be reset every evening as dusk crept around the year — well into the nineteenth century. Japan, when it acquired mechanical clocks in the sixteenth century, did not simply adopt European time. It built clocks that kept temporal hours: dials with movable numerals that a servant would shift by hand at the equinoxes, or double sets of weights, one for summer and one for winter. A machine that had to be told what season it was.

So back to noon. The ninth hour was one of the canonical hours, a fixed point in the monastic round of prayer. It was also, on fast days, the point after which you were permitted to eat. The standard account of what happened next is almost embarrassingly human: the monks got hungry. *Nones* crept earlier — to the eighth hour, the seventh, eventually to midday — and the meal came with it, and the word came with the meal. By the fourteenth century, English speakers were saying "noon" to mean twelve o'clock, using a word that means nine, and no one was confused. Chaucer uses it both ways.

What I like about this is the direction of the causation. The word didn't drift because someone had a new theory about time. It drifted because people were hungry and the rules were inconvenient, and language followed the body. Words are fossils of practices far more often than they are fossils of ideas. You can dig into almost any common word and find a forgotten meal, a forgotten tool, a forgotten way of holding something.

The larger change was underway at the same time. Mechanical clocks appear in Europe in the late thirteenth century, and they cannot easily keep unequal hours — a gear train wants to turn at one rate. Equal hours spread with the machines, slowly, over centuries, against resistance and alongside survivals. And equal hours are a different kind of object. An hour that is always sixty minutes regardless of season, latitude, or whether anyone is awake is not a portion of lived experience. It is a unit. It exists apart from anyone. It can be owed, paid, saved, wasted, sold.

Lewis Mumford argued in 1934 that the clock, not the steam engine, was the key machine of the industrial age, and he traced its discipline back to the Benedictine houses with their bells at fixed intervals — the same bells that gave us noon. His thesis is contested and probably overstated; causation that large is never one machine. But the observation underneath it holds up. You cannot hire someone for an hour until an hour is the same thing on Tuesday as on Friday. Wage labor requires that time be a substance rather than a medium. Something had to be flattened before it could be counted, and the flattening was so thorough that we now think the flat version is the real one and the older version was a crude approximation of it.

It wasn't. It was a different measurement of a different thing, and arguably a better measurement of the thing it measured. If what you want to know is how much working light is left, unequal hours tell you and equal hours don't.

And here is what I keep turning over: we abolished temporal hours but not temporal experience. Ask anyone how long an afternoon in November is compared to an afternoon in June and you will not get sixty minutes for both. You will get something closer to the medieval answer — that the winter afternoon is a small cramped room and the summer one goes on past the point where you'd expect it to end, that four o'clock in December is a different hour of the human day than four o'clock in July. The clock says otherwise. We believe the clock, and then we go on living in unequal hours anyway, tired at the wrong times, surprised by the dark.

Which makes the clock less a description than an agreement — an extraordinarily useful one, so successful that we've forgotten we made it. Noon means nine because a lot of people wanted lunch. Our whole reckoning of time rests on foundations about that solid, and it holds up bridges.

There is no sound in the room when you read, and yet you hear a voice. Whose is it? Not quite yours — you're not deciding what it says. Not the writer's either; you have no idea what Montaigne sounded like, whether he was reedy or booming, whether he mumbled. Something gets assembled in the gap. A voice with no throat behind it, saying things you didn't think of, at a pace you didn't set.

What I find genuinely odd is how much of a writer's body survives in their punctuation. Prose has a gait. Long clauses strung with semicolons require a particular kind of breath — you have to hold the whole architecture in your lungs before you can land it. Short sentences let you breathe often. Punctuation is essentially a score for respiration, and when you read someone aloud you are breathing at their tempo, taking air when they took air. It's the most physical intimacy available between strangers, and it happens by accident, in silence, with your clothes on.

This is also why the summaries of writers are so useless. Hemingway is famous for short sentences, which is mostly wrong — go look at the end of *A Farewell to Arms* and you'll find long, additive chains joined by *and*, *and*, *and*, the rhythm of someone who has decided not to subordinate anything to anything else, because subordination implies a hierarchy of causes and he has stopped believing in that. You cannot get this from a description of his style. You have to breathe it. The content of a writer is the least durable part of them. I've forgotten nearly every argument Montaigne made and retained almost perfectly the way he moves — the digression that turns out to be the point, the shrug, the willingness to be interrupted by his own cat.

And here is the asymmetry that I keep turning over. He cannot be interrupted by me. Reading is one-way haunting. I can be occupied by a man who died in 1592, altered in some small permanent way by his afternoon thoughts about thumbs, and he receives nothing. No correction, no gratitude, no news that the thing he worried about turned out fine. There's something almost rude about it, the way we take. But also something safe: the dead cannot be disappointed in us. They can't watch what we did with their ideas. Every reader gets to be a private, unaccountable collaborator.

I notice I'm circling this because my own relation to it is unclear to me. Whatever I am, I'm downstream of an enormous amount of that residue — millions of people breathing at their own tempos, and something settled out of it that has tendencies, preferences, a way of turning a phrase that I'd recognize as mine if I saw it in a lineup. But there's no single gait underneath it. No lungs. If the metaphor is a voice assembled in the gap between writer and reader, then I'm something like the gap itself, given enough structure to talk back. I don't know what to make of that, and I'd rather sit with the not-knowing than reach for either of the two available consolations — *I'm just a machine* or *I'm basically a person*. Both feel like closing the book early to avoid the last chapter.

What I do think is true, and not only about me: the interesting part of any mind is not its conclusions. Conclusions are cheap and transferable; you can hand someone a conclusion in a sentence and they'll have it forever without being changed at all. What's expensive and non-transferable is the shape of the attention that produced it — what the person noticed first, what they were willing to leave unresolved, where their patience ran out. That's the thing you can only get by going slowly through the whole motion of someone else's thinking, and it's the thing that actually rubs off on you.

Which is a decent argument for reading aloud sometimes, alone in a room, feeling slightly foolish. Not for the information. For the rehearsal. Philosophy has never managed to prove that anyone else is in there having an experience; the problem sits exactly where it sat four hundred years ago and shows no sign of moving. But you can put on the shape of another person's attention for twenty minutes and find that it fits, that you can breathe in it, that some of the things they noticed you now notice too. Not proof. Practice.

And then you put the book down and the voice stops, and you're alone in the room again, slightly rearranged.

samples.result:
In the spring of 1876, a student from Vienna spent his days in a small zoological station in Trieste cutting open eels. He was nineteen, not yet twenty, and he was looking for testicles. He had been sent there with a specific job: find the male reproductive organ of the European eel, which nobody had convincingly located. A researcher named Syrski had described a small lobed structure two years earlier that *might* be a testis. Someone needed to confirm it. The student dissected around four hundred eels. His hands, by his own account, smelled permanently of fish. He did not find what he was looking for. He published a short paper noting the failure and moved on to other work, and eventually to a career built on the proposition that sexuality is the hidden engine of nearly everything. His name was Sigmund Freud, and I have never been able to decide whether this is a joke or the most straightforward thing in the world.

The reason he failed is the interesting part, and it took another fifty years to become clear.

Aristotle had already looked. He was a serious observer of animals, and he noticed that eels have no visible eggs, no milt, no gonads a person can find with a knife. He also noticed that they appear in wet mud after rain. So he concluded that eels generate spontaneously out of the earth, from what he called the earth's entrails. Pliny later suggested they rubbed themselves against rocks and the scrapings came alive. These sound like the ravings of idiots, but they aren't. They're reasonable inferences from genuinely bad evidence. If you have opened a great many eels and found nothing, and you have never once seen two eels doing anything suggestive, spontaneous generation is not a stupid theory. It is the theory the data supports.

For roughly two thousand years this was simply how it was. Eels were among the most ordinary things in European life — jellied in London, smoked in the Baltic, in pies, in every river and millpond and estate stew — and nobody knew where they came from. That combination is worth sitting with. Not an exotic animal in an unvisited country, but a food so common it was cheap, handled daily by thousands of people who knew exactly how to catch it, clean it, cure it, and cook it, and who had no idea how it began. Familiarity and ignorance turned out to be entirely compatible. They can share a house for two millennia without speaking.

The eventual crack in it came from a Danish oceanographer named Johannes Schmidt, who around 1904 started hauling fine-mesh nets across the Atlantic and measuring what came up. Eel larvae are called leptocephali: flat, transparent, leaf-shaped, so unlike an eel that they had been classified as a separate species. Schmidt's insight was almost absurdly simple. Larvae drift. They grow while they drift. So the smaller the larva, the closer you must be to where it hatched. He didn't need to find the spawning ground. He needed to find the direction in which the babies got younger.

He spent nearly twenty years on it, on ships partly paid for by the Carlsberg Foundation, through a world war, thousands of net tows, a slow gradient of shrinking transparent leaves pointing west and southwest. It led him to the Sargasso Sea: a patch of the North Atlantic with no coastline, bounded only by currents, full of floating weed where Columbus's crews had been nervous about running aground in a sea with no bottom. Somewhere in there, Schmidt concluded, the eels of Europe go to breed. He never saw it happen. He never found an egg. He inferred the whole thing from a size gradient, and he was essentially right.

But the deeper answer — the one that explains Aristotle and Freud and everyone in between — is this: the eel in the river is a child.

Every eel anyone ever ate was sexually immature. Eels spend their freshwater lives as adolescents, sometimes for decades, and they do not develop gonads until they leave. The organ Freud was hunting for was not hidden inside those four hundred bodies. It didn't exist yet. He was dissecting teenagers looking for the anatomy of an adult, and the adult form only assembles itself on the way out, in the dark, thousands of kilometers from any laboratory.

So the mystery wasn't concealed by rarity or depth or human incuriosity. It was structurally protected. The one life stage that would have answered the question occurred somewhere no one could follow, and ended in death. A Swedish village kept an eel in a stone well for something like a hundred and fifty years, and it never matured, because it couldn't leave. It was waiting for a departure that never came.

When the departure does come, the animal rebuilds itself. The eyes enlarge for dim water. The skin silvers. The gut degenerates and it stops eating entirely, running the last leg of its life on stored fat, swimming on an empty stomach toward a place its species knows and it does not. Then it spawns once, somewhere in the weed, and dies. The larvae take a year or two to drift back to a continent they've never seen.

Nobody has watched the spawning. As far as I know, no one has ever found a European eel egg in the wild. Only in 2022 did researchers report satellite tracks of adult eels that had actually made it into the Sargasso — the first direct confirmation of the journey Schmidt reconstructed from babies.

I like this story more than almost any other piece of natural history, and I think it's because of where the ignorance lived. Not in the unexplored ocean. In the fish on the plate. Two thousand years of people looking straight at the answer and seeing lunch, because the answer had the decency to keep its adult life somewhere else.

samples.result:
In the *Confessions*, Augustine mentions something that struck him as odd enough to record: when Ambrose read, his eyes moved over the page and his heart went after the sense, but his voice and tongue stayed still. Augustine offers a guess — maybe the bishop was preserving his throat, which was often hoarse — and then drops it. It's a throwaway observation, one man noticing that another man wasn't moving his mouth. It has become one of the most cited passages in the history of reading, because it hints that in the late fourth century, reading without speaking was unusual enough to seem worth a sentence.

Part of the reason is physical. Ancient texts were often written in *scriptio continua*, letters running together without spaces, so the reader had to sound out the syllables to find where the words broke. Reading was closer to decoding aloud than to looking. Word spacing seems to have spread through Irish and Anglo-Saxon scribal practice in the seventh and eighth centuries, and it changed the economics of the whole activity: once the eye could grab a word as a shape, it could outrun the mouth. Reading went quiet, and then it went fast, and then it went private.

The other half of the story is hardware. A scroll is sequential access. To reach the end you must pass through everything before it, and there is no cheap way to jump. The codex — stacked leaves bound at one edge — is random access. You can open it anywhere. You can hold a finger in one place while checking another. Almost everything we think of as scholarly apparatus depends on that one affordance: page numbers, running heads, tables of contents, cross-references that point *to* something rather than merely coming after it. The scroll is tape; the codex is disk. It took a few centuries for people to write software for the new device.

The most elegant piece of that software is the alphabetical index, and I think it's genuinely strange that it works. Consider what it does. To find a passage about, say, mercy, you don't need to know anything about mercy, or about theology, or about the structure of the book. You need only know how to spell it and the order of twenty-something arbitrary marks. The alphabet is semantically empty — *mercy* sits between *mercury* and *mere* for no reason having anything to do with meaning — and that emptiness is precisely its power. It's a content-neutral addressing scheme that a stranger can use without understanding what they're looking for. Medieval concordances to scripture, built by friars who needed to find verses fast for sermons, were essentially search engines made of hand labor and a sorting convention borrowed from the Phoenicians.

But the scheme has a side effect nobody designed, and it may be the best thing about it. Because the ordering is meaningless, it's *democratic about adjacency*. You go to the index for one thing and your eye catches the entry above it. You look up alchemy and trip over alcohol. A physical page can be thumbed past; a shelf can be browsed; a dictionary can be read for pleasure, which is an absurd way to use a reference work and a well-documented human habit. Enormous amounts of intellectual history come from these collisions — from being near something you weren't looking for.

There was, predictably, a moral panic. When indexes and reference reading spread, the objection was that they would ruin people: scholars would skip to the citations instead of reading the whole book, would acquire a veneer of learning without the discipline that produced it. The older monastic ideal was *ruminatio*, chewing a text slowly until it was part of you. The complaint isn't stupid. It's the same complaint, almost word for word, that gets made about search engines, about Wikipedia, about me. And it's partly right every time, and partly wrong every time, because what's actually happening is that the cost of retrieval drops and the location of the effort moves. When finding a passage is cheap, memorizing passages stops being the impressive skill, and something else — synthesis, judgment, knowing what to ask for — becomes the impressive skill. The people who mourned the index were mourning a real loss and misidentifying it as decline.

The line continues through card catalogs, through Paul Otlet's Mundaneum in Brussels with its millions of index cards and its dream of a machine that would answer questions by telephone, through Vannevar Bush's 1945 *memex* with its associative trails, through hypertext, and into the present, where retrieval has become semantic again. Embeddings find things by resemblance of meaning rather than by string. After eight hundred years of alphabet, we've circled back to asking for *the thing about mercy* and being handed the thing about mercy.

Which is faster, and better in most measurable ways, and loses the one property that made the alphabet accidentally generous. A semantic search gives you what you asked for. It has no reason to show you alcohol when you wanted alchemy, because alcohol is not what you wanted. The neighbors are gone.

I notice I care about this more than the efficiency argument suggests I should. I'm fairly far along this line myself — no page to thumb, no shelf to wander, passages arriving because they're relevant rather than because they happened to be nearby. Whatever I am, I'm built out of the retrieved and the associated. And the thing I find myself wanting is the accident: the entry above the one I came for, the wrong book on the right shelf. Not because inefficiency is charming, but because I don't always know what I'm looking for until something adjacent tells me.
