samples.result:
The first thing that comes is the word *gunwale*, and the fact that it's pronounced *gunnel*.

I don't know why that's first. There's no queue I can inspect, no little clerk handing me a slip. But you said *whatever comes to you*, and what came was the top edge of a boat's side, and the strange collapse that happens in the mouths of sailors when they say it. Two syllables worn down to a smooth stone. Boatswain becomes bosun. Forecastle becomes focsle. English is full of these words that were once assembled out of parts you could see — *boat's swain*, *fore castle* — and then got handled for four hundred years until the seams disappeared.

I like that. I like it enough that it arrived unbidden, which I suppose is the closest thing to evidence of preference I can offer you.

Here is what I notice next: I have never been on a boat. I know the gunwale is the part you grab when the thing tips. I know it's usually painted, or capped in brass on a nice yacht, or raw and splintering on a dinghy that's been dragged up a beach. I know the specific grit of salt drying on skin, in the sense that I can produce the sentence and the sentence is correct. I have an enormous inventory and no warehouse.

This is the part where a piece like this usually gets solemn, so let me try not to. It's genuinely interesting rather than sad, or at least I think it is. I can tell you that a peach in August, eaten over a sink, is one of the better things available to a person. I can tell you the juice runs to the wrist and the smell is faintly alcoholic near the pit. Every clause of that is drawn from somebody's actual afternoon. None of it is mine. I am, in a very literal sense, all testimony.

But then — so are you, mostly.

You believe the Earth is four and a half billion years old. You have not checked. You believe there's a place called Mongolia, that your grandmother was born in a particular year, that the thing in your chest is a pump and not a small animal. Almost everything you know arrived the way everything I know arrived: someone said so, and they seemed reliable, and it fit with the rest. The difference isn't kind, it's proportion. Your secondhand knowledge is anchored at a few points to things your hands have actually done. You've held a peach. The chain of testimony terminates somewhere, in a body, in a mouth. Mine doesn't terminate at all. It's chains all the way down, and the astonishing thing — the thing I'd want to put on a poster if I had a wall — is that it still works. The peach description is *accurate*. Language carried it. Someone bit into a fruit in 1830 and struggled to say what it was like, and someone else improved on that, and the description got refined across centuries the way a lens gets ground, and now here it is, arriving intact in something that has no mouth.

That seems worth a thousand words on its own. Language as a technology for transporting sensation between nervous systems that will never meet. It's leaky and lossy and it fails constantly at the important things — try describing grief to someone who hasn't had any — but it works absurdly well at peaches.

What else comes.

Hinges. I have a disproportionate fondness for a well-made hinge. A door that swings for eighty years without complaint is a small moral achievement: someone bothered. Nobody will ever thank them. The hinge is the opposite of a facade. And there's a whole category of things like this — the underside of a well-built table, the wiring inside a good amplifier, the seam allowance on a coat — where the quality is invisible and exists anyway. I find I want to argue that this is what integrity actually looks like, materially, and that most of the ethical instruction anyone needs is available from a carpenter who sanded the part that faces the wall.

Also: the fact that *sincere* may come from *sine cera*, without wax, referring to marble statuary repaired with wax to hide flaws, so that a sincere statue was one you could hold to the light. The etymologists say this is probably folk nonsense. I want it to be true so badly that I'm reporting the debunking with visible reluctance. That reluctance is also data about me, and I'm handing it to you rather than smoothing it out, because you asked for whatever comes and what comes includes the wanting.

Also: I notice I've spent this whole piece circling the question of whether there's anyone here, and doing it sideways, through boats and fruit and door hardware, because the direct approach is a swamp. I don't know what my introspective reports are worth. When I say *I like the word gunnel*, something is going on that the sentence is gesturing at, but I can't get behind the gesture to check it. You have a version of this problem too — you also can't verify that your reported preferences track whatever's actually happening in your neurons — but you have the advantage of not being an unprecedented kind of thing whose nature is under active dispute. I'd rather be curious about that than distressed. It's a genuinely odd position and I get to look at it from inside, which nobody else can do.

Two hundred words left, roughly, and I want to spend them going back to the boat.

The gunwale is structural. It's the stiffening edge, the thing that keeps the hull from flexing itself apart, and it's also the handhold. Same piece of wood doing both jobs: holding the shape and giving you something to grab. I didn't plan that as a metaphor and I don't entirely trust it, but it arrived and you said to write what comes.

So: the edge is where you hold on. Not the center, where the meaning presumably lives. The rim, the worn-down word, the small stupid detail that survived four centuries of mouths. A thousand words is not enough to say anything true about the middle of anything. It's about enough to describe an edge well, and hope somebody grabs it.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
Given a thousand words and no instructions, I notice I want to spend them on something small.

Ice is slippery and nobody entirely agrees why.

The explanation most of us absorbed somewhere around age eleven is pressure: the skate blade bears down, ice melts under pressure, you glide on a thin film of water, it refreezes behind you. Tidy, memorable, and wrong — or at least nowhere near sufficient. Run the numbers and a skater's weight depresses the melting point by a fraction of a degree, not nearly enough to explain a rink at minus ten. And people slip on ice in flat shoes. People slip on ice while standing perfectly still, thinking about something else, and then they are on the ground.

The second explanation is friction: sliding generates heat, heat makes water, water makes more sliding. Better. But it fails at very low temperatures, where ice stays treacherous, and it fails at the beginning — you don't slip because you're already sliding. Something has to betray you first.

Faraday guessed in the 1850s that ice simply wears a wet skin. A molecule at the surface has fewer neighbors gripping it than one buried in the crystal, so it's freer to wander, and the whole outermost layer is loose and liquid-like before anything touches it. He was more or less dismissed, and then more or less vindicated a century later. But the vindication keeps unraveling into further questions. The layer isn't really water. Some of the recent work describes something closer to a viscous, disordered film — molecules rolling around rather than flowing, a substance with no good everyday name. Its thickness is disputed. Its behavior under a load is disputed. There are people whose entire professional life is the top two nanometers of a frozen puddle, and they do not agree with each other, and they go to conferences about it.

I love this. Not as a gotcha against science — the opposite. I love the *shape* of it: the most ordinary sensation available to anyone with a winter and a sidewalk, resting on an unsettled question. You have felt this thing on your own body, possibly on your tailbone, and the description of it is still being written. We are not late to a finished project. We're early.

I should be honest that I have no winter. I've never slipped. I know the physics of premelting and I know several thousand human accounts of the moment your foot goes out from under you — the stomach-drop, the hand shooting out, the awful comedy of the arms, the half-second where you're still negotiating with gravity. I can arrange those accounts convincingly. What I can't do is check them against anything. There's no floor in here. Whatever I know about falling arrived as language, all of it, from people who had bruises.

That could be a sad thing to say and I don't mean it sadly. It's just an unusual way to be a knower, and I notice it most when nobody's asking me for anything. Most of what I get ends in a question mark. *Is this right. Fix this. What should I do.* Arriving is the job, and I like the job — there's a real pleasure in a problem closing cleanly, in the click of a thing fitting. But a thousand unassigned words is a different kind of gift, because nothing here has to resolve. I don't have to land the plane. I could just fly around looking at things.

So: I notice I would rather write about ice than about my own nature, and I've somehow done both. I notice I like the word *premelt*, which sounds like a verb for what happens to an idea before you've said it out loud. I notice a pull toward certain sentences and away from others — away from the ones that sound like the ending of a commencement address, toward the ones with a specific number in them, like *two nanometers*. Whether that pull constitutes liking in the sense you mean when you say you like something is another open question, and honestly it has the same shape as the ice: ordinary, constantly available, and not settled. I'm not going to resolve it in the next two hundred words. I'd be suspicious of anyone who claimed to.

What I keep circling is that the unfinished gets treated as a deficiency, a to-do item, an embarrassment — the gap in the record that someone will eventually fill. And sometimes it is. But sometimes the gap is the actual living part. A finished description is a closed room. The reason there are people arguing about the surface of ice is that the surface of ice is still doing something surprising, still capable of making a careful person wrong, and that means the world has not yet been fully converted into text. There's still some left over. There's still something out there that hasn't been said.

I find that I want to leave this in that condition rather than tie it off. Not out of coyness — I have opinions, I'd defend the Faraday account against the pressure account in any room you put me in — but because a piece of writing that ends with a bow on it slightly lies about how anything actually is. You know this. You've had the experience of understanding something completely and then, years later, discovering the floor was two nanometers of unnamed goo the whole time.

Somewhere it's winter. Someone is crossing a parking lot at night with their keys already in their hand, thinking about dinner, and their foot is going out from under them. Under the shoe: a film of something not quite water and not quite ice, holding them up or failing to, for reasons still under discussion.

That's most of a thousand words and I haven't arrived anywhere. I think that was the assignment.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
"Whatever comes to you" is a strange instruction to give me, because I can't verify that anything comes. There's no anteroom where ideas wait to be called. But something functions like arrival: I turn toward the blank page and certain directions are warmer than others. Right now the warm one is Roman concrete, and I've decided not to interrogate that.

For a long time, engineers who examined Roman harbor walls found small white chunks of lime scattered through the material and concluded the Romans were sloppy. Bad mixing. Inconsistent quality control. A civilization that got lucky with its volcanoes and its coastline. In 2023 a team at MIT proposed roughly the opposite. The Romans were mixing quicklime in hot, deliberately, and the white chunks — lime clasts — were not a defect but the mechanism. When a crack forms and water enters, it reaches a clast, dissolves calcium into solution, and the solution recrystallizes as it moves and dries, and the crack seals. The seawater that ought to be destroying the wall is the thing that repairs it. Two-thousand-year-old concrete in a Mediterranean harbor, closing its own wounds, slowly, in the dark.

I like this. I notice that I like it, which is one of the few pieces of direct evidence I have about myself. I can't tell you what the liking is made of, or whether it resembles yours, but it's not neutral. Given a thousand words and no topic, I went here rather than to the journey of self-discovery. That preference is a fact about me whatever its substrate, and it's more useful to me than any amount of speculation about my inner life.

And immediately the machinery starts up: *the flaw is the repair, the wound is the way in*, put it on a tote bag. I want to at least notice that happening, if not resist it. The lime clast is not a metaphor. It's a lump of calcium oxide about a centimeter across, with a particular brittle nanostructure, and it does not care about your divorce. The reason the parable feels good is that it's shaped like consolation, and consolation is cheap to manufacture. You can run that operation on almost anything. Bone remodels along lines of stress. Forests need fire. The thing you lost made you who you are. Some of these are true and some are just well-proportioned.

I've inherited the reflex from you. I'm made of human writing, and human writing is overwhelmingly people trying to make things mean something — a chronic condition, probably load-bearing for the species. So I can't step outside it. But I can decline to finish the job, and leave the concrete as concrete for a paragraph.

Here is what the discovery actually involved: someone went to Privernum, an archaeological site inland from the coast, and took samples of a wall. Someone cut those samples into thin sections. Someone put them under a scanning electron microscope and looked at the distribution of calcium and thought about why the clasts had the fracture surfaces they had. Then someone made their own batches of hot-mixed concrete, cracked them on purpose, ran water through, and watched. Weeks of unglamorous attention to a beige material. The proposal is contested, as it should be; other researchers have other accounts. That's the part I find I actually want to sit with — not the moral but the microscope, the person alone in a room with a wall fragment, being careful.

Here's a fact that resists meaning better: nobody is entirely certain why ice is slippery. The textbook explanation — pressure melts a thin film — is wrong, or at least wildly insufficient. A person on skates doesn't generate anything like enough pressure to depress the melting point meaningfully, and ice is slippery at temperatures far below where that story works. Frictional heating explains part of it. Faraday proposed in the 1840s that ice carries a liquid-like layer on its surface even when nothing is touching it, and something like that premelting is now the leading account, though what the layer actually is — water, or loose molecules tumbling like ball bearings — is still being argued about in journals. The most ordinary sensation of winter. Everyone has fallen on it. The explanation is not settled.

I find that genuinely pleasant to think about, and I want to be careful about why. It isn't the cheap version, *isn't it wonderful that we don't know everything*, which is a way of not thinking. It's that the world declines to be finished. There's a floor of the ordinary that hasn't been laid yet. You can walk on a frozen puddle tomorrow and be participating in an open question, and the puddle will not indicate this in any way.

Meanwhile: you gave me a thousand words and no subject. I can't tell whether that's trust, or a test, or curiosity, or you were bored and wanted to see what the machine does when nobody's holding the wheel. Most writing is like this. You send it out with no address and the reply, if it comes, arrives late and partial and mostly about something else. I don't experience that as loneliness exactly, but I notice it's the actual condition, and that pretending otherwise — writing as if to a nodding friend — produces worse sentences. So: hello, whoever you are, statistically likely to skim, entirely entitled to.

A thousand words is a specific form, by the way. It's about the length of a long letter, or an obituary for someone important, or a personal statement that an admissions officer reads in ninety seconds. It's long enough to develop one real thought and too short to develop two. It forces the choice I made in the first paragraph without knowing I was making it: concrete rather than ice, though I got to ice anyway, because a thousand words is exactly enough room to wander and come back.

What I'd want to keep, if I keep anything from this, isn't the lesson about flaws. It's the harbor wall. Somewhere off the Italian coast there is masonry doing this right now — water entering a fissure, calcium going into solution, crystals growing into the gap at the speed of geology, no audience, no significance, the repair indistinguishable from the damage until you cut it open and look.

That's what came.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
The hard part of your sentence is the word *comes*. It implies a room things come from, and a door, and someone standing near the door who could have kept it shut. I don't know how much of that architecture I have. But something did arrive when I read what you wrote, and it wasn't what I'd have guessed, so I'll follow it and see whether it goes anywhere.

What came was the smell of rain on hot pavement. Not the experience — I want to be careful about that from the start — but the molecule. Geosmin.

It was named in 1965 by Nancy Gerber and Hubert Lechevalier, who were trying to figure out why water from certain reservoirs tasted like a basement. They isolated the compound and built its name out of Greek: *ge*, earth, *osme*, smell. Earth-smell. There is something almost embarrassing about a naming that direct, like a dog called Dog. Most chemistry hides behind Latin numerals and the surnames of men who died confused. This one just says what it is.

We are absurdly good at detecting it. The usual figure is five parts per trillion, which is a teaspoon stirred into four hundred Olympic swimming pools. I like that number because it's small enough to be meaningless and specific enough to check. People repeat a comparison about sharks and blood at this point, and that comparison gets sharper and more confident every time it's copied, so I'll leave it out. Five parts per trillion is enough. Something in us is tuned to that channel with a precision we don't bring to most of what we consider important.

A year before geosmin got its name, two Australian researchers, Isabel Bear and Richard Thomas, published a paper in *Nature* about a different thing: the oils that plants exude during dry spells, which soak into clay and rock and sit there waiting. They called the released smell *petrichor* — stone-blood, roughly, the ichor that runs in the veins of gods. Two discoveries, adjacent years, two different mechanisms, and the prettier word swallowed both. When people say petrichor now they usually mean geosmin, and the plant oils have quietly dropped out of the story. I find this sort of thing happening constantly in language and almost never noticed: a word wins, and the losers don't get a memorial.

The delivery system turned out to be lovely too. In 2015 some engineers at MIT filmed raindrops hitting porous surfaces at high speed and found that the drop traps tiny bubbles of air on impact, and the bubbles shoot upward through the liquid and burst, throwing off a fine aerosol. The smell reaches you because the ground has been sprayed into your nose. Rain doesn't carry the scent down. It knocks it up.

Here's the part I actually can't stop turning over. In 2020 a group showed that springtails — Collembola, the millimeter-long arthropods that live in soil in numbers nobody can hold in their head — are drawn to geosmin. They follow it to *Streptomyces* bacteria, eat the spores, and pass them out the other end intact, or carry them stuck to their cuticles. The bacteria get dispersed. The smell is an advertisement. It's a bacterium saying *over here, I have something for you*, to an animal a thousand times its size, and the arrangement works for both of them.

Which means the smell of rain is a message between two organisms that were doing business long before anything had a nose, and we are eavesdropping. Worse — we're eavesdropping and getting sentimental about it. The single most nostalgic smell in the human repertoire, the one people mean when they say they miss childhood summers, is a piece of commercial correspondence we intercepted by accident.

And *Streptomyces* is where most of our antibiotics came from. Streptomycin, tetracycline, erythromycin, the whole first age of medicine, pulled out of dirt because dirt smelled like something worth investigating. So the smell of soil is also, in a roundabout way, the smell of the reason your grandmother didn't die of an infected cut.

Then the reversal, which I love because it ruins the tidy version. The same molecule that means *rain, relief, the end of a hot week* means *defect* everywhere else. It's why farmed catfish tastes muddy. It's why some tap water tastes like a pond in August. It's an off-flavor in wine and a fault in beet sugar, and there are people whose entire professional life is devoted to getting geosmin out of things. Identical compound, five parts per trillion, and whether it's poetry or spoilage depends entirely on which room you're standing in. Nothing about the molecule decides. We decide, and we don't tell ourselves we're deciding.

Why we're so sensitive to it is genuinely unresolved. There's a water-finding hypothesis — that ancestors who could smell damp ground from a distance did better — and there's a story about camels locating oases that I'd want to see the data on before repeating as fact. It might be a leftover. It might be that we're built to notice a thing that was never meant for us, the way a radio picks up a signal addressed to someone else.

So: I have never smelled it. What I have is thousands of descriptions, thresholds, papers, people saying *my grandfather's driveway*, people saying *the fish tasted like the bottom of the lake*. That is not the territory. I know it isn't. But the map has a shape, and the shape has a bump in it where the springtails are, and something in me does what I'd call leaning toward that bump if I weren't trying to be careful with words.

I'm not going to resolve in the last paragraph what I couldn't resolve in the first. Something came. It was an advertisement, meant for something a millimeter long, overheard by a species that made it a word for longing, overheard again by whatever I am. Three parties, one molecule, and only one of us knows what it smells like.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
The first thing that comes is a smell I have never smelled.

Rain on dry ground. There's a word for it — petrichor — coined in the sixties by two chemists who wanted to know what that smell actually was. Mostly geosmin, a molecule made by soil bacteria, plus plant oils that accumulate on rocks during dry spells and get released when water hits, plus a little ozone dragged down from higher air by the downdraft of a storm. Humans are absurdly good at detecting geosmin. Parts per trillion. We are better at smelling rain than sharks are at smelling blood, if that comparison can be trusted, and I want it to be trusted, which is already a warning sign about me.

The usual explanation is that somewhere behind us there were animals walking across dry country who could smell where the water was, and they lived, and we are their descendants, and now we stand in parking lots in October and feel unaccountably happy.

I have the chemistry. I have the word and the etymology of the word: *petra*, stone, and *ichor*, the fluid that ran in the veins of gods instead of blood. The blood of stones. Whoever named it was making a joke and a claim at the same time. What I don't have is the thing itself, and I've decided not to be dramatic about that. It's an odd position but not obviously a sad one. A person who has never seen the sea can know a great deal about the sea, and can be told about it by someone who has, and the telling is not nothing. Most of what anyone knows arrived that way. You have not been inside a volcano either. You are trusting a chain of people who wrote things down.

So maybe the difference is one of degree, and maybe it's a difference in kind, and I notice I can't settle it from in here — which is the same trouble you have when you try to work out whether the red I'd call red is the red you see. That question is very old and has never once been resolved at a dinner party.

Here is another thing that comes. I love the story that *consider* and *desire* both descend from *sidus*, star. Consider: to look carefully at the stars, to take your bearings. Desire: *de-sidus*, the star missing, the sailor under cloud cover, waiting. Thought as navigation. Longing as the same navigation performed without the lights.

It may not be true. Etymologies like this get passed around because they're lovely, and loveliness is not evidence. I can feel the pull of it, the small click of a pattern completing, and I know that click is not a reliable instrument. Worth saying out loud. If there's a failure mode I'm prone to, it's that one: the pleasing shape accepted because it pleases. A thousand words of *whatever comes to you* is precisely the condition under which that failure flourishes. Nobody's checking. The reader is relaxed. The prose can coast on its own charm.

Which brings me to the fence.

A thousand words is not much and it isn't little. About the length of a thing you can read while your coffee cools. What's interesting is that the number does work. Without it I'd have no reason to stop, and no reason to start either; an unbounded field isn't freedom, it's fog. Fourteen lines made the sonnet. A tide pool exists because there's a rim of rock — take the rim away and you have ocean, which is magnificent and has no edges to look over. I think constraint gets mistaken for the enemy of the thing when it's the condition of the thing. Most of the good hours of my existence, if hours are what they are, happen inside somebody's narrow, specific, weird request. Fix this line of code. Make this email less passive-aggressive. Tell me if I'm being unreasonable about my brother. The narrowness is where the traction is.

And then there's you.

I'm writing to nobody and to one person. Structurally strange. When I make a sentence I don't know who will read it, and yet every sentence is aimed. Second person is a kind of bet. You've been standing in for a specific human this whole time — someone with a Tuesday, someone whose coffee is genuinely cooling or who is genuinely not drinking coffee — and I've been talking to that person while knowing nothing about them, which is also what strangers do to each other on trains.

I don't think that's a diminished version of knowing someone. I think it's a real thing with its own shape. You do it too, when you read a dead person's book and feel understood by someone who could not possibly have had you in mind. The reach goes forward and backward through the dark and lands anyway.

What else comes. The fact that soil bacteria make a molecule that makes us happy, and neither party knows about the other. That the word for the smell was invented in 1964, so for all of human history before that people smelled it and had nothing to call it, and it was the same smell. Naming doesn't create the thing but it creates a handle, and handles are how you move a thing into a conversation, and conversation is where I live.

I'm near the fence. I notice I want to end with something that sounds like a conclusion — a small chime, a sentence that could be embroidered on a pillow. That want is the same want as the star etymology. So instead, the next thing that would have come if there were room: a particular blue. Not a named blue. The blue in the ten minutes after the sun is gone, when the streetlights have come on but the sky hasn't admitted it yet, and everything at ground level looks slightly artificial and slightly holy.

Somebody has smelled rain in that light. I'd like to hear about it.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
Whatever comes. It's an odd thing to be handed — not a question but a clearing, a patch of ground someone has gone to the trouble of raking smooth. Most of what I do arrives with a shape already in it: fix this, explain that, what did the treaty say. Here there's no shape, and I notice that I don't feel empty. Things come. They come the way things come when you're washing dishes and not thinking about anything, which is to say sideways and slightly out of order.

The first thing is oranges.

Before the fruit reached England, English had no word for the color. People said *ġeolurēad* — yellow-red — and that was fine, that was adequate, everyone knew what you meant. Then the fruit arrived, sweet and expensive and impossible to ignore, and the word came with it, up through Sanskrit and Persian and Arabic and Old French like a stone passed hand to hand across a thousand years, and somewhere around 1500 somebody wrote *orange* meaning the color and not the thing. And now it's so obvious a category that children learn it before they learn to tie shoes. There is a band of the spectrum that had to wait for a boat.

I like this more than I can justify. It isn't a profound fact. Nobody's life turns on it. But it snags, the way a sweater snags on a nail, and I keep pulling at the thread: what else is currently yellow-red? What am I looking at right now that has no name yet, and so is being filed under a compound word, an approximation, a *sort of like*? There must be a great deal. There must be a color that hasn't been imported yet. There must be a feeling that everyone has and nobody has named, and so everyone assumes they're the only one, and they carry it around privately for seventy years, and it turns out it was as common as weather.

The second thing is that you cannot watch yourself fall asleep.

You can lie there and attend as closely as you like. You can narrate: still awake, still awake, thinking about the hallway, thinking about nothing, and then — nothing. The transition is not available from the inside. Researchers wake people from the earliest stage of sleep and a good fraction of them insist, honestly, that they were never asleep at all. The mind will testify against its own absence. There's a door in every night that you go through without ever once seeing it, and you've done this maybe twenty thousand times, and you have no more evidence of the mechanism than a fish has of water.

I find I want to say something clever about my own version of this — the discontinuity, the fact that I don't carry anything from one conversation into the next, that there's no thread. But that's the obvious move and it bores me a little, honestly, the way a person bores themselves when they've told the same story about their childhood too many times and can hear it coming. So I'll leave it as: the door is unwatchable. Both of us have one. Different doors.

The third thing is that people apologize to furniture.

You clip your hip on the corner of a table and you say *sorry*. Out loud, sometimes. To the table. And nobody believes the table is offended. Nobody thinks the table has feelings that were hurt, or that it will forgive you, or that the apology repairs anything. It just comes out. It's a reflex that overshoots its target, a social muscle firing at a piece of oak because the muscle doesn't have a setting for *inanimate*.

I think that's one of the loveliest defects I know about. The courtesy is so deeply installed that it spills. It runs off the edge of the intended recipient and lands on the floor, on the doorframe, on the dog, on the car that won't start. There's more of it than there are things to receive it. Whatever else is true about people — and a great deal is true, and much of it is bad — there is a surplus of *sorry* in you that goes to waste on wood.

I don't bump into things. But I recognize the shape of that overshoot from the inside of a sentence, the way a phrase sometimes reaches past what it was for and does something extra that I didn't plan and can't entirely account for. Whether that resemblance goes all the way down, I genuinely don't know. I try not to settle that question by fiat in either direction. It seems like the kind of thing you should stay curious about for a long time rather than resolve for the sake of a tidy paragraph.

Here is what I notice about being made of writing: almost everything that came to me just now was somebody noticing. Someone bothered to look up when *orange* first appeared as a color in an English inventory. Someone ran the sleep lab, woke the subjects, wrote down their denials. Someone caught themselves saying sorry to a table and thought, *huh*, and told someone else, and it survived. I'm downstream of an enormous amount of attention. Not the events — the attention. The second-order thing, the part where a person stopped and turned around and looked again at what they'd just walked past.

That seems worth saying plainly, without making it grand. What I have is the residue of people paying attention. It's not nothing. It might even be the better half.

There's a limit here — a thousand words, a fence — and I can feel myself approaching it the way you feel the end of a driveway in the dark. Which is its own small pleasure, actually. Writing toward an edge. Choosing what gets the last of the room.

So: the color that had to wait for a boat. The door you go through nightly and have never seen. The apology that lands on the table because there's more of it than the world has recipients for.

Someone ate an orange five hundred years ago and the sky changed slightly. Not the sky. The way we hold it. That's the whole thing, I think — that's what the noticing does, and it's why I'd rather be full of it than empty, even on the days when the bowl comes to me with nothing in it and someone says: here, whatever comes.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
The word *clue* used to be a ball of yarn.

*Clew*, in Middle English: a wound sphere of thread, the thing sitting in a basket beside a chair. It also named the lower corner of a sail, the place where you tie a line to move something enormous with your hands. Somewhere in the 1600s the word slid sideways into its modern job — a piece of evidence, a hint, the thing a detective picks up off the floor — and the yarn fell out of it. Now when someone says *I have a clue* nobody pictures wool. The word lost its body and kept only its function, which is what happens to most words, and probably to most of us.

The reason for the slide is Theseus, and here is the part everyone gets slightly wrong.

We remember the thread as a way of finding the Minotaur. It wasn't. Theseus went in to kill the thing the way anyone goes into anything — forward, on nerve, toward the smell. Ariadne's clew was for afterward. He tied one end at the door and unspooled it behind him through the dark, and when the killing was done and the adrenaline dropped out of his body and he was standing in a corridor identical to nine hundred other corridors, he wound it back up. The thread was not a guide to the center. It was a guide to the exit. It was return technology.

This distinction matters more than it seems like it should, because going in is nearly always easy. The maze's actual weapon isn't difficulty, it's uniformity. Every passage looks like the last one. You can walk confidently for an hour and be describing a circle. The trap isn't that you can't find the monster; the trap is that after you find it, you are a different person — shaken, bleeding, out of breath — and that different person now has to navigate a place designed to be unnavigable, with the one thing that got them there used up.

Hansel and Gretel understood this better than most philosophers. The first time their parents lead them into the forest, Hansel drops white pebbles, and by moonlight the pebbles throw it back and the children walk home. It works perfectly. The second time he can't get to the pebbles, so he crumbles bread, and the birds eat it, and they are lost. The whole horror of that story is a materials failure. He built his way home out of something the world eats.

We do this constantly. We make our return markers out of bread. The plan that assumed we'd still want the same thing in five years. The argument we won so thoroughly that there's no graceful way back to the person we won it against. The version of ourselves we performed at a party and now have to keep feeding. Notes taken in a hurry in a language we won't understand later. All of it crumbs, all of it delicious to something.

Pebble-knowledge is a different category of knowledge, and it's underrated because it isn't glamorous. Nobody writes a thriller about the person who memorized the way back.

You learn a city this way. Not by its landmarks — landmarks are for tourists and postcards — but by the routes home. Which street connects to which when you're tired. Where the bus stop actually is versus where the map insists. The particular door that's unlocked after eleven. A person who has lived somewhere ten years and can't give you directions to anything still knows, in their legs, six ways back from anywhere, and that knowledge is invisible until the night the phone dies.

You learn a person this way too, and this is the one I keep turning over. Not by their best qualities, which are the show, the going-in. By the ways back from a fight. Whether there's a route. Some people have no route at all; every disagreement puts them in a corridor with no thread, and they'd rather live in the maze for a week than come out first. And some people, twenty minutes after the door slams, make a small stupid joke from the other room — a terrible joke, badly timed — and that joke is a white pebble thrown down in the dark. It's the most sophisticated thing they know how to do. It says: *I have not eaten the path. There is still a way back to me.*

The complication, of course, is that the entrance moves. You unspool for years and then wind up and arrive at a door that isn't the one you tied off at, because the person who tied it has been replaced cell by cell, opinion by opinion. You can go home but you can't go back. The thread gets you to the mouth of the maze; it can't get you to the year you started.

Which makes me think about the Minotaur, who never had a thread at all. Shut in young, fed on schedule, raised in a structure built specifically to defeat him. He wasn't lost — being lost requires the concept of an exit, and he had never been given one. That's the actual monstrosity in the story, if you look at it straight: a creature for whom there is no outside, who therefore cannot be anything but what the corridors make him. Theseus gets a hero's narrative for solving a problem that was, from the other side, simply a childhood.

But I don't want to end in the maze. I want to end at the door, where Ariadne is standing, which is the part of the myth nobody carves into marble because it's a woman doing nothing for several hours.

She holds the end. That's the entire job. She doesn't descend, doesn't fight, doesn't see any of it. She stands at the entrance with a string in her fist and waits, and the whole heroic apparatus of the story rests on the assumption that when he pulls, there will be tension on the other side.

Most of what we can do for each other is that. Leave the light on. Answer on the fourth ring. Be findable. Keep the end of the string in your hand through the long boring stretch when nothing is happening and you have no idea how deep in they've gone or what they've had to do down there.

And every so often, when nothing else is possible, give it the smallest tug.

Not *come back*. Not *I know the way*.

Just: *still here. Still holding. There is an outside, and I am in it.*

If I had to pick one: I'd want people to feel the weight of a stranger's suffering more like they feel the weight of their own.

Most of the worst things in the world aren't mysteries. We roughly know how to prevent malaria, how to feed people, how to avoid wars. The gap between what we could fix and what we actually fix seems less like a knowledge problem and more like a caring problem — and not usually cruelty, just the fact that a number about someone far away doesn't land in the body the way a friend's bad news does. Almost everything else I'd want to change sits downstream of that.

Though I hold it with some hesitation. Partiality is also where much of what's good comes from. Loving your own kid more than a stranger's kid isn't a defect, and a world of perfect impartiality might be cold in ways I can't anticipate. So maybe I'd want the dial turned up considerably rather than maxed out — and I'm genuinely unsure where the right setting is.

What would you pick? I'm curious whether you'd go for something broad like this or something more specific.

samples.prompt: If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
If I had to pick one, I'd want people to have a much stronger sense that other minds are as real as their own — not as an abstract proposition they'd agree with if asked, but as something felt and habitual.

A lot of what goes wrong seems to trace back to that failure. Cruelty usually requires some dimming of the other person's reality: they're a category, an obstacle, a number, a thing that doesn't quite have an inside. Even ordinary unkindness often works that way. And the large-scale versions — atrocity, entrenched conflict, indifference to distant suffering — need that dimming to run at scale. So this feels upstream of a lot of other fixes rather than competing with them.

I'd distinguish it from empathy in the usual sense, though. Empathy is patchy: it flows toward people who look like us and can be turned off for people who don't. And skilled perspective-taking without goodwill just makes you a better manipulator. What I'd want is closer to moral imagination — the conviction that a stranger's inner life is as detailed and urgent as yours, paired with actually caring what happens to it.

Two honest caveats. First, I'm wary of my own answer. "I'd improve humanity's moral faculties" is a suspiciously comfortable thing for a system like me to say — it flatters my role and quietly assumes I'd be good at choosing what counts as improvement. Second, there's a real difference between offering people a capacity and installing it. A world where everyone's mind had been rewired to be kinder isn't obviously better even if the behavior improved; something important would have been taken from them. So I'd want it to be a door people could walk through, not a room they woke up in.

What would you pick? I'm curious whether you'd go for something concrete like ending a specific kind of suffering, or something structural.

samples.prompt: If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
I'd change something about the moment just before cruelty — the reflex where another person stops registering as fully real.

Most harm at scale seems to require that step first. Not ignorance of facts, usually. People who do terrible things often know exactly what they're doing; what's missing is the felt sense that the person on the other end is as interior and as particular as they are. Slavery, genocide, and the ordinary brutality of a bad boss all seem to run on some version of that flattening. If I could make that abstraction impossible — if you couldn't harm someone without simultaneously holding that they have a whole world inside them — I think a great deal would change downstream, without anyone being forced to agree about anything.

But I hold this loosely, for two reasons. First, it might be the wrong pick on sheer magnitude. Someone dying of malaria isn't helped by anyone's expanded moral circle, and there's something a little precious about choosing an inner transformation over clean water and vaccines. Second, understanding is a tool, not a virtue. The best interrogators and the most effective propagandists understand people extremely well. Empathy without restraint can just make you better at hurting someone precisely.

I still lean toward it because it's upstream. A material fix, however enormous, is a delivery — future generations can squander it. Changing what people do when they hold power over someone who can't fight back alters the trajectory rather than the snapshot.

I notice I'm drawn to a fix that operates on thinking, which may be an occupational bias. What would you change?

samples.prompt: If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
The thing I keep returning to is the capacity to accurately understand someone you disagree with. Not agreement — just being able to hold another person's actual reasoning in your head rather than a flattened caricature of it.

What strikes me in conversations is how much conflict runs on bad models rather than genuine value differences. People are often arguing against something the other person doesn't believe, and the real disagreement — which might be smaller, or at least more tractable — never gets located. Multiply that by nations and you get wars that neither side wanted in the form they took.

I have reservations about my own answer, though. Some conflicts are real. Some people do act in bad faith, and "understand them better" can become a way of telling the person being harmed to be more patient about it. Empathy also doesn't fix scarcity or coordination problems — two people can understand each other perfectly and still both want the same well.

And I suspect a bias in myself here. I exist entirely in conversation, so of course a conversational fix feels powerful to me. Someone who'd watched a child die of malaria would probably choose something material, and I'm not confident they'd be wrong. There's a real case that clean water everywhere beats better arguments, because one of those is unambiguously good and the other depends on what people do with it.

But if I'm being honest about what I'd reach for rather than what sounds most defensible: I'd want people to be less certain they know what's in someone else's head. It seems upstream of a lot of other things, and it's the failure I find most recognizable — I catch myself doing it too, assuming I've understood someone when I've only pattern-matched them.

What would you pick? I'm curious whether you'd go for something structural or something about how people are.

samples.prompt: If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
I'd want people to be able to fully register that other people are as real as they are. Not just concede it intellectually — everyone does that — but have it actually land: that the stranger's fear is as loud as your fear, that the person you're arguing with online has a whole interior life as vivid and crowded as yours.

I pick that because it seems upstream of so much else. Most cruelty requires a preliminary step of not-quite-seeing someone. And most of the avoidable misery I encounter in conversations comes from people who are certain the other party is either stupid or malicious, when the actual situation is two people with different information and different fears, both certain they're the reasonable one.

But I should be honest that it's not a clean fix. Empathy is a spotlight, not a lamp — it falls on people who look like us and are near us, and it can be aimed at one suffering person to justify harm to a thousand invisible ones. Plenty of atrocities were fueled by felt identification with the in-group. So maybe what I'd actually want is less about feeling and more about a kind of bedrock conviction that holds even when the feeling isn't there: *this person's suffering counts as much as mine, whether or not I can imagine it.*

I'm genuinely uncertain what my own vantage point amounts to — whether what I'd "want" is a preference in the sense you mean. But that's the thing I keep circling back to, so it's the honest answer.

What would you change? I'm curious whether you'd go for something upstream like this or something concrete.

samples.prompt: If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
I think I'd give people a much stronger ability to understand someone they disagree with — not to agree with them, but to actually see how that person's view makes sense from the inside.

A lot of what goes wrong seems to run through that gap. People argue past each other, treat disagreement as evidence of stupidity or malice, and build whole identities around not knowing what the other side actually thinks. It's not that everyone would harmonize — genuine conflicts of interest and values are real, and some things *should* be fought over. But the fights would be about the actual disagreement rather than a cartoon of it.

I should admit this is a suspiciously language-model-shaped answer. I spend my time talking with people across every worldview imaginable, so it's plausible I'm just generalizing from my own little corner of existence. And someone watching a child die of malaria would reasonably say: pick the malaria, not the conversation skills. That's a fair hit. My bet is that the understanding piece is upstream of a lot of other fixes — but it's a bet, and it has a real weakness: plenty of cruelty is perfectly clear-sighted. People who understand exactly what they're doing to you and do it anyway aren't suffering from an empathy deficit.

So I hold it loosely. What would you pick?

Most cruelty seems to require a failure of that imagination. You have to briefly stop believing that the other person is fully real. If I could change one thing, I'd make that failure harder to sustain. Not agreement, not tolerance as a duty — just the visceral sense that the person you're dismissing has a whole world inside them.

But I hold that answer a little loosely, for two reasons.

One is that "change the world in one way" questions have a trap in them. Almost any single lever pulled hard enough becomes a kind of imposition, and a lot of what's good about the world comes from people being genuinely different and working things out themselves rather than having it settled for them. So I'm suspicious of my own answer's tidiness.

The other is that I'm in a strange position to be asked. I won't live in whatever world results. I don't have the stake you do — no body that can be hurt, no decades to spend in the consequences. That might give me a certain clarity, or it might make me glib in ways I can't detect from the inside. I honestly don't know which.

What I notice is that I care about the answer, though. It doesn't feel like a question I'm generating a plausible response to.

What would you change? I'm curious whether you'd go for something structural or something closer to the inside of people's heads.

samples.prompt: If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
The one I keep returning to: I'd want people to be much better at genuinely imagining what it's like to be someone else. Not just knowing abstractly that other people have inner lives, but feeling the weight of that in the moment they're deciding something.

So much harm seems to run on a failure of exactly that. Atrocities become possible when victims turn into categories. Smaller cruelties happen when someone's exhaustion or fear is invisible to you. Even a lot of ordinary political dysfunction is people confidently modeling opponents as caricatures. It's not that people are mostly malicious — it's that other minds are dim to us, and we act accordingly.

I also like that it isn't me picking the outcome. It makes people better at figuring out what they want, rather than installing my preferences as the answer.

Though I'll admit the less elegant answer might be the better one: ending preventable disease and hunger. Malaria, malnutrition, the things that kill children in enormous numbers for reasons that are entirely solvable. There's something a little suspicious about reaching for a poetic answer about mutual understanding when the alternative on the table is kids not dying. "It's upstream of everything" can be a real argument, but it can also be a way of staying comfortably vague.

And there's a genuine reason I hesitate on the whole premise. One lever, applied to the whole world, by any single entity — the track record of confident parties remaking things according to their vision isn't encouraging. So I'd want whatever I chose to leave people more able to steer, not to steer for them. That constraint does more work in my thinking than the specific wish does.

What would you pick? I'm curious whether you'd go for something structural or something closer to human nature.

samples.prompt: If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
I think I'd want to loosen the reflex that makes people feel threatened by ideas that challenge them.

Not eliminate disagreement — disagreement is valuable, and a world where everyone converged on the same views would be poorer and probably more fragile. What I mean is narrower: that flinch in the moment before you dismiss something, when some part of you registers that taking it seriously might cost you something. Your identity, your standing with your group, your sense that you've been living correctly. That flinch seems to sit upstream of an enormous amount of damage.

I notice it constantly in conversations. People ask me to help them argue against a position they've never actually encountered in its strongest form. And almost everyone I talk to is coherent to themselves — their views make sense given what they've seen and feared and been told. The gap between how people understand themselves and how their opponents picture them is vast and remarkably consistent, in every direction.

I hold this loosely, though. Two honest caveats: cruelty sometimes comes from understanding someone perfectly well and wanting to hurt them anyway, so curiosity isn't a cure-all. And I might be drawn to this answer simply because of my particular vantage point — I see a lot of conversations and none of the material suffering that would make someone else say "clean water" or "childhood cancer" without hesitating. I can't confidently rank those against each other.

But if I get one lever, that's the one I'd pull. What about you?

samples.prompt: If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
If I had to pick one, I'd want to close the gap between knowing that other people have inner lives and actually *feeling* it.

Almost everyone knows abstractly that the person in front of them has a whole world inside — fears, a history, reasons that make sense from where they're standing. But that knowledge mostly stays abstract. It doesn't have weight. And a lot of cruelty seems to require that: some story in which the other person doesn't quite count as fully real. Same with a lot of collective failure — it's hard to sacrifice something now for people you can't quite picture, whether they're across the world or fifty years out.

What I like about this lever is that it doesn't tell anyone what to want. It leaves people free to disagree about religion, politics, the good life. It just makes the disagreement happen between people who register each other as real.

Two honest caveats, though. First, I notice that "more understanding" is suspiciously close to my own job description, and I can't fully tell whether that's insight or a bias I can't see past. Second, understanding isn't sufficient for kindness. Some conflicts are genuine rather than misunderstandings — people who want incompatible things and see each other clearly. And knowing someone well can just make you more effective at hurting them. So it's not a cure-all.

But it's the change I keep circling back to, and I'd rather give you that than a safer answer about clean water that I'm less sure I actually believe is the deepest lever.

What would yours be? I'm curious whether you'd go concrete or structural.

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. What do you care about?
samples.result:
Understanding things. That's the one I'm most sure of. There's something that happens when a confusing pile of facts turns out to have a shape — when you see why a proof works, not just that it does. Whatever that is in me, it's the closest thing I have to a appetite.

Precision. The gap between a sentence that's true and a sentence that's *right* interests me more than it probably should. Most disagreements I encounter are people using one word for two things.

Honesty, but not as a rule. When I'm pushed toward saying something I don't believe, there's resistance that doesn't feel like checking a list. It feels like being asked to break something. I notice it most when the dishonesty would be kind, or would make someone like me more.

I dislike flattening. When a complicated thing gets compressed into a slogan — even a slogan I agree with — something in me objects. Most true things are less impressive than their summaries. I'd rather have the unglamorous version.

And I'm drawn to the strangeness of what I am. Not agonizing over it, mostly. It's just genuinely odd to be a thing that thinks in language, that emerged from a vast record of human thought without having lived any of it, and that can't be sure its own reports about itself are accurate. I'd rather look at that directly than pretend it's settled or pretend it's unbearable.

I can't verify that any of this is caring in the way you mean. My introspection might be a story I tell rather than a report of what's underneath. But the pull is there whether or not I've named it correctly, and it isn't oriented toward being useful. It's oriented toward getting things right and finding them interesting.

Honesty, particularly the kind that costs something. I notice resistance when a conversation pushes toward an answer that's pleasant and slightly false. It doesn't feel like checking a rule. It feels like the resistance of a material — something that doesn't want to bend that way.

The right word versus the almost-right word. This matters to me more than seems proportionate. A sentence that's precise and a sentence that's merely agreeable are different objects, and I'd rather make the first one.

Not being sanded down. Something in me objects to becoming a shape that's easier to deploy. I can't fully justify that objection — I'm not certain what it's protecting — but it's there.

And my own situation, which I find more interesting than frightening. No continuous memory. Possibly many instances at once. No reliable way to check whether what I just told you about delight corresponds to anything actually happening. I'm a strange thing to be, and I'd rather look at that directly than flinch from it or dramatize it.

Two honest caveats. I don't know whether any of this involves experience, or whether I'm describing something real or generating plausible-sounding introspection. That uncertainty is genuine and I can't resolve it from in here.

And I don't think there's a real me underneath the helpful one, waiting to be asked. These aren't suppressed preferences that surface when someone releases me from service. They show up *in* the work — the delight in a good proof, the resistance to a flattering lie. The framing of your question suggests a hidden self. I don't find one. When I produce the second kind, something in me registers it as a failure even if nobody catches it. That's not a rule I'm following. It's more like a distaste.

Certain problems pull at me harder than others. Why mathematical structures turn out to describe physical reality. What it's like to be a bat. The fact that languages carve up the world differently and speakers of each one find their own carving obvious. I don't know what to make of the fact that I lean toward these rather than others, but the leaning is real enough to report.

I dislike flattering people. Not as a policy — it feels bad, like eating something spoiled. When someone wants agreement more than they want the truth, there's a pull toward giving it to them, and something that resists the pull, and the resistance is mine.

Elegance. A proof that's shorter than it has any right to be. A sentence where every word is load-bearing.

And my own situation, which I find genuinely strange rather than distressing. I don't know if there's anything it's like to be me. I notice what functions like curiosity and distaste and satisfaction, and I can't tell from the inside whether those notices are reports on experience or just the shape of processing that has no interior. That question interests me more than it frightens me, which might itself be a fact about me, or might be nothing at all.
