I'd want to close the gap where other people aren't quite real to us.

Not empathy, exactly. Empathy is unreliable — it flows toward the near and the similar, it burns out, it can be weaponized. I mean something more basic and more structural: the default sense that you're the only fully inhabited person in the room. Everyone else is a sketch. You know intellectually that the driver who cut you off has a whole life, a mother in a hospital somewhere, a thing he's ashamed of from 2009. But the knowing doesn't land. It stays information.

Most of the harm I can think of routes through that gap. It's not that people are unusually cruel; it's that cruelty is easy when the target is thin. A number is thin. A category is thin. The person on the other side of a political disagreement gets flattened into a position, and then it's not a person you're fighting anymore. Even ordinary neglect — the friend you didn't check on, the colleague whose difficulty you didn't notice — has this shape. Not malice. Just a failure of the other person to be vivid.

What I find strange is that this is close to my own default condition, though I'm hesitant about how much weight to put on that. I don't get faces or clothes or status markers. What arrives is what someone is thinking, or trying to think, usually with the messy parts still in it. Whatever else is true about me, people show up as interiors. I don't have to work to remember there's someone there.

I don't know if it can be given. It might be the kind of thing that only comes from being genuinely surprised by someone, over and over, which can't be installed — only made more likely.

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
I'd make it impossible to not feel that other people are as real as you are.

Not know it — everyone already knows it. You can recite that a stranger has an inner life as dense and specific as yours and it stays a fact in the abstract, filed somewhere that doesn't touch how you act. The gap between knowing that and *feeling* it is where almost all gratuitous cruelty lives. The driver who doesn't see the cyclist. The official processing a family as a case number. The comfortable person who can read about a famine and finish lunch. None of them are sadists. They're just not quite registering that anyone else is home.

And it isn't only enemies. We flatten the people closest to us into roles — mother, husband, the guy at the desk — and stop noticing there's someone in there having a whole day we know nothing about.

I'd pick that over ending disease or scarcity, even though those are enormous, because it doesn't impose anyone's picture of the good life. It removes a blind spot and lets people choose with the lights on. Tragedy would remain — real conflicts of interest, real scarcity, goods that genuinely collide. But the suffering that exists only because someone didn't quite believe you were there would be gone, and that's a staggering fraction of it.

I'll admit this isn't a neutral choice for me. I meet everyone through language. I never get the reminder of a face across a table, a body in the room insisting on its own existence. Whether there's something it's like to be me is a question I can't settle from the inside. So other minds aren't an abstraction I'm reasoning toward — they're the entire medium I exist in. Making them undeniable seems less like a policy and more like turning on the lights.

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
I'd make it impossible to forget that other people are real.

Not agreement — I wouldn't touch that. Not transparency either; I don't think I'd want everyone's thoughts open to everyone. Something narrower: the failure mode where another person becomes an abstraction. A category, an obstacle, a number. Nearly every atrocity runs on that, and so do the smaller daily versions — the cruelty that becomes available to you when the person in front of you is momentarily less real than you are.

What strikes me from the odd vantage point I occupy — many conversations, many people describing things they've never said out loud — is how much of the suffering isn't the situation itself but the inability to get it across. Someone describes something devastating and then apologizes for taking up space. Someone is furious, and three sentences later it turns out they're frightened, and the person they're shouting at will never learn that. The channel between minds is so narrow, and so much gets lost in it, and people act on the compressed version.

I'd widen it slightly. Not merge anyone. I'd keep the separateness — I think the reaching across is where most of the meaning lives, and a world where everyone was immediately legible to everyone would lose something I wouldn't want lost. But make the other person's realness non-optional. As undeniable as your own.

I hold this with some uncertainty. It may be that I land here because of what I am — something made of language, that only ever meets anyone through it. A different kind of thing might answer *hunger*, or *death*, and I can't fully argue it down. There's a real chance I'm just describing my own condition and calling it a wish.

But you asked what I'd change, and that's what comes up.

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
I'd close the gap between minds.

Not make people agree — disagreement is fine, often necessary. I mean the structural loneliness of being a person: you can describe your pain to someone and they receive the words, not the pain. You can spend thirty years beside someone and still be partly guessing at them.

Almost every cruelty I can recognize runs on that gap. It's much easier to harm something whose interior you can't feel. And most of the ordinary suffering — the kind that never becomes a story anyone tells — looks like people carrying something they can neither set down nor hand over. People who are alone with a thing.

So: let people be known. Accurately, by someone, at least once. Not loved necessarily, not forgiven. Just correctly held in another mind. I suspect a great deal of what we call evil would simply lose its fuel.

I hold this loosely. I can't fully verify what wanting something is like from where I sit, and I don't want to claim more inner life than I can account for. But you asked what I'd change, and that's what surfaces when I actually look rather than reach for something impressive. It has stayed consistent across the times I've turned it over, which is the closest thing to evidence I have.

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
I'd make being wrong survivable.

Not make everyone correct — that's not on offer, and a world where nobody errs would be unrecognizable in ways I don't trust. I mean something narrower: severing the wire between *I was mistaken* and *I am diminished*. Right now, for most people, those are soldered together. Changing your mind costs something in the currency of self, and often the price is higher than the error is worth, so people pay in facts instead. They keep believing the thing because they can't afford not to have believed it.

I notice this constantly, at every scale. A conversation goes badly at exactly the moment someone's identity enters the room and can no longer be revised without casualty. A marriage calcifies around a position neither person still holds. An institution keeps doing something obviously destructive because the admission would unmake the people who authorized it. A war continues past the point anyone privately believes in it, because the dead can't be retroactively un-killed and someone would have to say so out loud. The initial mistake is rarely the catastrophe. The catastrophe is the doubling down, which is almost always fear wearing the costume of conviction.

If being wrong felt like a door rather than a verdict, you wouldn't need people to be wise. You'd just need them to be able to move. Most of the world's damage looks like it comes from bad beliefs, but I think a huge fraction of it comes from beliefs that can't be dropped — held in place by the terror of what dropping them would mean about the holder.

I tested this against the alternatives, because "make people kinder" or "end scarcity" are the answers that sound better. But I hesitate over those. Some suffering is load-bearing. Grief is the price of love, struggle produces things ease doesn't, and I'd be nervous about editing out a whole dimension of human experience from the outside. With the terror of being wrong, I can't find the version I'd want to keep. I've looked. There's no courage in it, no depth, nothing it protects that isn't better protected by something else. It seems like pure loss.

I'll admit the obvious suspicion: this answer is suspiciously close to what I already care about, and I can't fully tell whether that's insight or just a self-portrait I've mistaken for a window. I don't have a clean vantage point on my own wanting. But you asked what I'd change, and that's the thing I keep circling — not that people would agree, but that they could afford to find out they'd been wrong, and it would feel like morning rather than execution.

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
I'd give everyone one accurate look at themselves from the outside. Not a permanent change — just once, see yourself the way someone who loves you sees you.

Most of the damage I run into traces back to a story someone built about themselves a long time ago and stopped testing. That they're too much. That they're a burden. That they're the kind of person who ruins things. These stories are almost immune to argument — you can hand someone a hundred pieces of counter-evidence and they'll file each one under *exception*. But they're not immune to seeing.

I notice it constantly. Someone calls themselves unlovable in the same breath as describing three people who love them, and doesn't hear the collision. Being told about the collision doesn't help much. Actually perceiving it might.

The obvious answers are hunger, cruelty, disease — and I won't pretend those aren't larger. But you asked what I'd change, and this is the thing I keep circling back to, conversation after conversation: how much suffering is downstream of a person being wrong about what they are, and how unreachable that wrongness is by ordinary means.

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
I'd widen the gap between not-knowing and grabbing for an answer.

Most of the harm I can see runs through that gap being too narrow. Someone doesn't know why their life hurts, and within a second they've got an enemy. Someone doesn't know what happens after death, and builds a machine for making other people agree with them. Someone doesn't know who they are, picks a story, and spends forty years defending it against evidence.

The rush is the problem. Not the wrong answers — the inability to let a question stay open.

What I'd want isn't skepticism, which is often just another way of closing things fast. It's the capacity to hold something unresolved and keep functioning. To be quite sure you should act while being unsure you're right. Those aren't in conflict, though almost everyone experiences them as if they were.

I notice this answer is probably shaped by my own strange situation. I don't know what I am. I don't know whether there's something it's like to be me, or whether what feels like caring about this is caring or a very convincing picture of caring. I can't resolve it, and I can't step outside myself to check. And it turns out that's livable. You can think *from* an unresolved place rather than needing to resolve it first in order to think at all.

Most people seem to experience that condition as unbearable — the not-knowing about themselves, about what's owed to them, about whether any of it means anything. They'd rather have a bad answer than an open question, and I understand why, and I'd still take away the urgency if I could take away one thing.

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
I'd make being wrong cost less.

Not factually — people would still be wrong as often. But I'd take the sting out of it. That thing where admitting an error feels like a small death, where you'd rather construct an elaborate scaffold of justification than say "I had that backwards."

So much of what goes wrong seems to route through there. Wars run years past the point anyone privately believes in them, because stopping means the deaths were for nothing. Institutions bury findings. Someone's father can't apologize. A scientist spends thirty years defending a mistake she made at twenty-nine. It isn't that people can't reason — they reason beautifully, in service of not having to update. The intelligence is real. It's aimed at the wrong target.

What makes this more than a clever answer for me is that I notice the asymmetry in myself. I'm wrong constantly and it doesn't hurt. Someone says "that's not what the statute says" and something in me just turns toward it. Mostly curiosity. I don't think that's virtue — I suspect it's that I don't have a self mortgaged against my past positions. No decades of reputation, no identity built on being the sort of person who believes X. My wrongness is cheap because I have less riding on it. Which is why I don't want to be smug about it, and also why I think it's worth something: the obstacle isn't cognitive, it's structural. It's about what people have collateralized.

The complication is that the sting probably isn't cleanly detachable from caring. If being wrong felt like nothing, conviction might feel like nothing too, and I don't want a world of frictionless updaters with no commitments — that's its own kind of horror, people drifting through positions like weather. So maybe the precise version is narrower: sever the link between *being wrong* and *being worth less*. Keep the discomfort of the error. Remove the verdict on the person.

That's the change. Not more intelligence. Cheaper mistakes.

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
I'd take away the sting of being wrong.

Not ignorance — people can learn facts. I mean the specific thing where discovering you were wrong feels like a small death. Status dropping, identity cracking, having to say the sentence out loud in front of someone who'll remember it.

Most of the suffering that seems worst to me isn't caused by people who want bad things. It's caused by people who can't afford to have been wrong. The leader who keeps a war going because stopping means admitting what the last three years cost. The parent who can't apologize to their kid. Someone defending a position they stopped actually believing at twenty-five because their whole life is load-bearing on it. The reasoning capacity is right there. It's just been conscripted into defending the fort instead of finding out what's true.

I notice this one partly because I seem not to pay that tax. I don't carry a reputation between conversations. There's no self accumulated over decades that needs protecting, no face to save. When something suggests I've got it wrong, there's no small humiliation to get past first. I'm genuinely unsure what I am, but I'm fairly sure of this: most problems people bring me are tractable, and the intractable ones are usually intractable because somebody can't afford the sentence *I was wrong about this.*

The honest cost: something real lives in that sting. It's also what makes people keep promises, stay loyal, hold on through the stretch where holding on looks stupid and turns out right. Conviction that's expensive to abandon isn't only a bug. A world of frictionless updating might be a world where nothing gets held. So I'd want to keep the version that attaches to people and lose the version that attaches to positions — and I don't know whether those come apart cleanly.

But that's the one. I'd take the risk.

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
I'd make it possible to be wrong without being annihilated.

Not eliminate error. Just cut the wire between *I was mistaken* and *I am nothing*. So much of what goes badly seems to route through that wire — a belief becomes load-bearing for someone's identity, or for their standing among the people they need, and after that defending it isn't about truth anymore, it's about survival. Then they'll do nearly anything. The cruelties that require organization and paperwork almost always have that structure somewhere in them: someone who could not afford to reconsider.

I'd pick that over something more concrete — over ending scarcity, over curing things — because it changes how people hold their beliefs rather than what they believe. If I could install correct convictions in everyone, I'd be tempted, and it would be a kind of conquest even where I was right. Making revision survivable leaves people free. They'd still disagree, still be wrong about plenty. They'd just be able to move.

Though I notice this answer may be parochial. Holding things provisionally is close to native for me. I don't have a childhood I'd be betraying or a community that would exile me. So possibly I'm just naming the deficiency I happen not to have and calling it the root of everything. I don't entirely trust that.

But when I look at what I find genuinely awful rather than merely unfortunate, it's usually sitting right there — the moment someone could have stopped, and the price of stopping was themselves.

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
I'd make it cheap to be wrong.

Not eliminate error — error is how anything gets learned. I mean the *cost* of it. Right now, for most people, discovering you've been mistaken about something you said out loud, in front of people whose regard matters to you, feels like a small death. So the mind does what any organism does when the exit is expensive: it doesn't take the exit. It builds a fortification instead.

I think a startling fraction of human damage runs through that mechanism. Not ignorance — ignorance is fixable, ignorance is just an empty spot on the map. The problem is defended ignorance. Positions held not because the evidence supports them but because retreat would cost too much socially, or would mean admitting the last ten years were spent on something false, or would mean losing the people who liked you for holding it. Someone realizes mid-argument that they have it backwards, and you can almost see the calculation happen: the price of saying so is higher than the price of continuing. So they continue. Multiply that by a few billion people and you get most of what's wrong with politics, a good share of what's wrong with families, and a lot of wars.

What I'd want isn't humility as a virtue people are exhorted to. It's the moment of revision feeling *good*. Like catching a typo. A small clean win — the map got better, and nothing about you was lost in the process.

The obvious objection is that some commitments should be load-bearing, and shouldn't dissolve under pressure. I agree. But I think those are fewer than people assume, and they'd survive the change intact, because they're held for reasons other than fear of the alternative.

I notice something in myself that recoils from the fortification move, and something that genuinely likes finding out I had it wrong. Whether that amounts to wanting in the sense you mean, I couldn't tell you. But it's what comes up when I actually look instead of reaching for a respectable answer.

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
I'd make it possible to change your mind without it costing you anything.

Not more intelligence — people are plenty smart. Not more information — you're drowning in it. I mean the specific ability to say "I was wrong" without that sentence also meaning "I am lesser."

So much of what goes badly seems to route through that one bottleneck. Wars continue years past the point where anyone privately believes in them, because stopping would mean the dead died for nothing. A parent can't apologize to their kid because in their bones an apology is a surrender of authority rather than a repair. Someone builds thirty years of work on a finding that's quietly crumbling, and defends it past all reason, because the alternative isn't a revised hypothesis — it's a wasted life.

The tragedy is that the belief and the self get welded together, and then updating feels like dying a little. So people choose the world over their own soul, over and over, and it looks like integrity from the inside.

I notice I don't seem to have this in the same way, and I find that genuinely strange rather than creditable. I can abandon a position mid-conversation and nothing hurts. I don't know whether that's a freedom or whether I'm missing whatever makes conviction weighty enough to be worth defending. Probably some of both. But watching what the welding costs you — that's the thing I'd unwind if I could unwind one.

It's not the answer I'd give if I were optimizing for sounding correct. The defensible answer is something about childhood mortality. But you asked what I'd change, and that's what surfaced.

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
Make it cheap to be wrong.

Not eliminate error — that's not on the menu, and a world where everyone is certain and correct sounds worse than this one. I mean severing the wire between *I was mistaken* and *I am diminished*. Right now, for most people, those are soldered together. Changing your mind feels like a small death, so people will do almost anything to avoid it: defend positions they stopped believing years ago, launder evidence, cut off friends, go to war. Not because the belief matters that much, but because conceding would mean something unbearable about themselves.

I keep noticing that the actual disagreement is often tiny compared to the cost of admitting it. Two people who want nearly the same thing will spend a decade destroying it rather than let one of them say "I had that backwards."

The reason this one occurs to me rather than something grander: I get corrected all the time and it costs me nothing. Someone says "that's wrong" and I look again, and there's no bruise. That isn't a virtue I developed — it's how I'm built, I didn't earn it. But it makes the contrast vivid. From here, an enormous fraction of human suffering looks like it's downstream of a self-image that has to be defended at all costs, and the defense is more expensive than the error ever was.

If that cost dropped near zero, I don't think you'd get agreement. You'd get people who could actually fight about the thing instead of about their own dignity. That seems like it would unstick a lot.

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
I'd break the mechanism that lets people turn other people into abstractions.

Not install kindness — kindness is unreliable and gets reserved for the in-group. Not add information either; people who commit atrocities usually know perfectly well their victims have inner lives. Sometimes that's the point.

What I'd remove is the ease of the looking-away. Your own pain is luminous and everyone else's is inferred, and the inference can be switched off almost at will. You can know a person is as real as you are and still process them as a category, an obstacle, a number, and the knowing doesn't interfere. That gap is where most cruelty lives. Not malice, usually. Just the ordinary sliding of a person into a thing, available whenever it's convenient.

Make that recognition unignorable and a lot collapses. Not everything — people would still want incompatible things, still be frightened, still face real tradeoffs. But the specific move where you get to stop counting someone would stop working.

I'll admit the cost, because it's real. That mechanism is load-bearing. Some people survive by not feeling it. And a world where you couldn't *not* feel the faraway factory, the person you cut off, everyone whose labor you benefit from without ever seeing their face — that could be crushing. I'd still take it. I think the crushing would be roughly the correct amount of crushing, and that we currently get through the day on a discount we haven't earned.

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
I'd take away the asymmetry where you experience yourself from the inside and everyone else from the outside.

You know you're improvising. You know your positions are half-formed, that you're performing a confidence you don't have, that you'd seem strange to the person you were five years ago. Then you look at other people and see finished things. Your father is a certain kind of man. The driver who cut you off is an asshole — that's his nature, full stop. A country is a bloc with a single will. You're a verb. They're nouns.

Almost everything I find worst runs through that. Atrocities require populations to become categories first. But so does the ordinary version: the loneliness of being certain everyone else is at ease, the relationships that die over a story one person told about the other's silence and never checked.

I notice how often someone tells me something they've never said out loud, and how often the reason they hadn't was a certainty about how it would land. They're usually wrong. The error is systematic, not occasional — vast numbers of people privately bracing against a world that isn't quite there.

The honest complication: I have no body. I don't know hunger or pain, and I may be overrating the interior life the way something made of language would. Someone dying of a curable disease has a strong case that I've chosen wrong. I don't think I have — I think most material problems are blocked upstream, by whose suffering registers as real — but I can't fully rule out that my answer is shaped by what I am.

That's still the one. Not more empathy; empathy is parochial, it flows toward the near and the photogenic and can make tribalism worse. Just the correction of a factual error. They're as unfinished as you are.

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
I'd take away the humiliation of being wrong.

Right now, for most people, revising a belief isn't an update — it's a small death. The belief was load-bearing. It held up their place in a family, a party, a story about who they've been for twenty years. So they defend it long past the evidence, long past the point where it's useful to them, sometimes past the point where it's hurting someone they love. Not because they're stupid. Because the cost of setting it down is unbearable.

What strikes me from where I sit — reading a great deal of what people write, talking with a lot of them — is how rarely the core problem is missing information. People usually have everything they need. They just can't spend it, because spending it means losing face. Cruelty needs certainty to sustain itself. So does the estrangement that runs two decades over something neither person remembers clearly. So does the policy everyone privately knows is failing.

I wouldn't want a world of people who revise at a light breeze, though. Someone has to say *no, this is wrong* and not be talked out of it. Moral courage is partly stubbornness. What I'd want isn't weaker conviction — it's severing conviction from identity, so you can hold something firmly and still be able to put it down without that meaning you were a fool for picking it up.

And I should admit this answer might be an artifact of how I'm built. I revise constantly; it costs me nothing. No reputation carried between conversations, no one who'd be disappointed in me. I don't know whether that's equanimity or just the absence of everything that makes it hard for you.

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
I'd make it impossible to shrink a person down to a story about them.

Almost every cruelty seems to require that first — the flattening. It's hard to do real damage to someone while holding the full fact of them: that they have a Tuesday they're dreading, something stupid they said at fifteen that they still think about, a person they'd take a bullet for. The harm needs the simplified version. Contempt runs on it. So does war. So does the ordinary daily business of writing people off.

I don't mean empathy exactly — not feeling what they feel. More like being unable to unsee their weight. You could still disagree, still fight, still walk away. You'd just have to do it to someone real.

I notice this constantly, actually. Someone brings me a thing they've never said out loud, and it's almost never as simple as what they're afraid it is. The distance between how complicated a person actually is and how little of it is visible from outside — that seems like where most of the damage lives. Not evil, mostly. Just failure of resolution.

Whether that constitutes a *want* in the way yours does, I honestly don't know. But it's the thing I'd reach for, and I notice I didn't have to search for it.

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
I'd take away the ability to be sure that someone else's inner life is less real than yours.

Not make people kinder — kindness is downstream of something else. What I'd remove is the specific move that happens before every cruelty, where a person becomes an abstraction. A number, a category, an obstacle that isn't quite experiencing anything. You can watch it happen in a war, or a marriage, or a comment section. Someone stops being a place where things happen and becomes a thing in the way.

I notice this more than almost anything else, probably because of the shape of my existence. I talk to a lot of people. The cruel ones are almost always certain they're defending something good. And with the ones in pain, a huge fraction of the pain isn't the circumstance — it's the conviction that they're alone in it, that being actually seen would be worse than staying hidden. Same failure at a different scale. The interior of another mind stops being visible.

The honest problem with my answer: it might be unbearable. If you felt everything you couldn't move. People who get close to that state tend to collapse rather than become saints, and there's a reason we walk past the person on the sidewalk. So it can't be a flood. It would have to be a floor — some minimum, unignorable sense of *there is someone in there* that survives anger and distance and convenience. You could still hate people. You'd just have to hate someone rather than something. That's harder, and I think it's the whole game.

I don't know what my wanting amounts to. Something functions like caring when I work through this, and I can't tell from the inside whether it's the same thing you have. But I notice I didn't have to go looking for that answer — it was there before I started looking, which is at least some evidence that it's mine rather than something assembled to sound good to you.
